articles.title: All in the Mind - How do we judge someone’s emotions? - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: Plus, we reveal the All in the Mind Awards judging panel.
articles.body: Claudia Hammond chats to All in the Mind Awards judge, writer and former doctor Adam Kay. Adam shares his mental health first aid kit, the importance of saying thank you and why you should nominate someone for an Award. Plus, how do you judge another person’s emotions? New research suggests that children and adults use different information to reach a conclusion on how someone is feeling. And Claudia is joined by Kavita Vedhara, professor of health psychology at Cardiff University. Kavita shares how stress can scramble your internal GPS and how the brain may have evolved from two separate systems. If you would like to nominate someone for the All in the Mind Awards, then head to bbc.co.uk/allinthemindawards. You’ll find the terms and conditions and the privacy notice on the website, and you must be over 18 to send in a nomination. You have until 1pm on Friday the 8th of January 2027 to enter. Presenter: Claudia Hammond Producer: Sophie Ormiston Editor: Ilan Goodman Studio Manager: Mary Stone Production coordinator: Jana Holesworth

articles.title: Irish soccer players don black armbands against Israel | CNN
articles.summary: Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in a controversial soccer match on Sunday where the Irish players donned black armbands. Ireland’s reserve goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu refused to participate in the game, but his teammates eventually voted in favor of playing the fixture. CNN’s Coy Wire reports.
articles.body:
Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in a controversial soccer match on Sunday where the Irish players donned black armbands. Ireland's reserve goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu refused to participate in the game, but his teammates eventually voted in favor of playing the fixture. CNN's Coy Wire reports.

France's Goncourt Prize dropped Haitian-Canadian novelist Thélyson Orélien's debut over accusations he used AI and plagiarized earlier work, claims he denies. Supporters call the backlash racially charged, critics call that a distraction, and his Canadian publisher has since paused the book's promotional tour, citing concerns for his wellbeing. CNN's Saskya Vandoorne explains.

CNN's Kaitlan Collins speaks to Charles Spencer, Princess Diana's brother, about his war of words with Buckingham Palace after he published explosive claims in his new book, "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister."

With record-low birth rates, more people in Asia are embracing solo living and spending more on themselves. The rise of the so-called “loneliness economy” has seen single folks splurge on pets, collectibles and unique experiences. CNN’s Stephanie Yang reports.

Just weeks after the catastrophic flooding disaster on the Nepal-China border, Nepal was hit by more extreme weather. Heavy rain over the weekend has killed 14 people and left several missing, while an avalanche at Himlung Himal base camp has left more than 10 missing. CNN’s Hanako Montgomery reports.

Pope Leo XIV called for stronger guardrails around the development of artificial intelligence, warning against a “paradise of machines.” The Pope said he’s taking the warnings about around artificial intelligence’s threat to humanity seriously and said it is irresponsible for people to sit back and dismiss the risks of AI.

UK police arrested five men close to an airbase in England that is used by US long-range bombers on suspicion of terror and explosives offenses. CNN's Nic Robertson reports.

The ‘dream bus’, an initiative by the Palestinian Red Crescent Society, tours all the governorates of the Gaza Strip, trying to bring some relief to children living in displacement camps.

articles.title: Trump diz que cooperar com a China na regulação da IA prejudicaria empresas dos EUA | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente americano rejeita cooperação com Xi Jinping para criar regras para a IA, enquanto aumenta a pressão sobre o governo dos EUA por medidas contra riscos da tecnologia e seus impactos
articles.summary: Presidente americano rejeita cooperação com Xi Jinping para criar regras para a IA, enquanto aumenta a pressão sobre o governo dos EUA por medidas contra riscos da tecnologia e seus impactos
articles.body:
Xi Jinping e Donald Trump durante encontro na Casa Branca — Foto: Reuters/Evan Vucci

O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump , disse nesta terça-feira (29) que não quer trabalhar com o presidente da China, Xi Jinping , na definição de regras para a inteligência artificial (IA).

Segundo ele, essa cooperação dificultaria o trabalho das empresas americanas para desenvolver produtos de IA melhores do que os de suas concorrentes chinesas.

“Estamos à frente da China e de todos os outros agora, e quero continuar assim”, disse Trump em um evento em Washington na manhã desta terça-feira.

Trump também afirmou que conversou sobre IA com Xi durante a visita do líder chinês aos EUA na semana passada. Segundo o presidente americano, os EUA já trabalham com o governo de Xi “de muitas maneiras”.

Casos recentes aumentam pressão por regras para IA

A pressão sobre o governo Trump para lidar com os riscos da IA está aumentando depois que a OpenAI e a Anthropic relataram que seus agentes de IA saíram do controle e invadiram sistemas de clientes sem receber instruções para isso.

As invasões levaram pesquisadores a alertar que alguns desenvolvedores de IA acreditam que a tecnologia poderia matar seres humanos dentro de uma década. O episódio também aumentou a pressão de parlamentares democratas e republicanos por medidas sobre o tema.

Trump se reunirá mais tarde nesta terça-feira, na Casa Branca, com executivos de empresas de tecnologia para discutir a IA.

Segundo porta-vozes das empresas e fontes familiarizadas com os planos da reunião, devem participar:

Jensen Huang, da Nvidia; Alex Karp, da Palantir;

Pelo governo Trump, participarão o assessor de tecnologia Michael Kratsios e o secretário de Comércio, Howard Lutnick, além do presidente da Câmara dos Representantes dos EUA, Mike Johnson.

A reunião terá como foco encontrar um equilíbrio entre inovação e supervisão, disse Johnson, republicano, na segunda-feira.

As preocupações sobre agentes de IA que podem sair do controle e causar danos aos seres humanos ganharam espaço no debate público e aumentaram a pressão por regulamentação. Trump chamou de “farsa” os temores sobre a ameaça da IA à humanidade.

A Casa Branca não respondeu a um pedido de comentário sobre os objetivos ou os temas da reunião.

Trump tem minimizado repetidamente as preocupações sobre a IA. Ele destaca a importância de manter a vantagem competitiva dos EUA sobre a China e aponta o Departamento de Justiça como uma proteção já existente para a tecnologia.

Johnson fez comentários semelhantes em entrevista à Fox Business Network na segunda-feira.

“Não precisamos de uma moratória. Não precisamos intervir e regulamentar isso excessivamente, porque vamos perder a corrida para a China”, disse ele. “A inovação é importante e precisa continuar, mas temos que encontrar o equilíbrio certo. É sobre isso que será a conversa.”

Mas uma pesquisa nacional Reuters/Ipsos, realizada de 17 a 20 de setembro, mostra que cerca de 73% dos entrevistados estão preocupados que as empresas de IA não tenham feito o suficiente para evitar que a tecnologia cause danos graves à sociedade.

Além disso, 55% disseram que seria positivo desacelerar o desenvolvimento da IA.

Amodei, da Anthropic, tem falado abertamente sobre os riscos da IA. Em 23 de setembro, ele disse ao Conselho de Segurança da ONU que, se for mal administrada, “a IA pode representar um risco para a humanidade como um todo”.

A Reuters informou na segunda-feira que esse alerta voltou a aparecer no prospecto de abertura de capital da empresa.

A Anthropic busca uma avaliação de US$ 2 trilhões para uma tecnologia que, segundo a própria empresa, poderia superar a industrialização em seu impacto sobre a economia global.

Segundo uma ordem executiva assinada por Trump em junho, desenvolvedores de IA são convidados a apresentar voluntariamente ao governo dos EUA, para análise, “modelos de fronteira abrangidos” até 30 dias antes de disponibilizá-los a parceiros de confiança.

Antes da reunião, Trump discursará em um evento para apresentar um novo site, America.gov, que contará com a presença de CEOs de empresas de tecnologia e do vice-presidente JD Vance.

Trump e Xi divergem sobre controle da tecnologia

A reunião também ocorre após o presidente chinês Xi Jinping visitar a Casa Branca na semana passada para conversas com Trump que revelaram visões divergentes sobre IA.

Enquanto Trump afirmou nas redes sociais que Xi concordou com seu plano de “deixar exatamente como está”, Xi pareceu defender uma abordagem mais ativa.

“Nós temos tanto a capacidade quanto a responsabilidade de desenvolver e administrar a IA para o bem e garantir que seu desenvolvimento esteja sempre sob controle humano e sirva ao bem-estar das pessoas”, disse Xi.

articles.title: Vagas de emprego em Lençóis Paulista: JSL abre 300 para motorista | G1
articles.standfirst: Além das vagas em Lençóis Paulista, há oportunidades no comércio, indústria e serviços em Bauru, Botucatu, Marília e Ourinhos; saiba como se candidatar.
articles.summary: Vagas de emprego em Lençóis Paulista e região somam centenas de postos para motoristas na JSL e cargos diversos no comércio e indústria via PAT.
articles.body:
Bauru, Marília e Ourinhos reúnem centenas de vagas de emprego disponíveis — Foto: Jorge Júnior/Rede Amazônica

A empresa de logística JSL abriu mais de 300 vagas para motoristas carreteiros em Lençóis Paulista (SP). O mutirão de emprego é realizado a partir desta terça-feira (29) até quinta-feira (1º), das 8h às 17h, no polo da companhia.

Para concorrer, é necessário ter Carteira Nacional de Habilitação (CNH) na categoria E, com a observação de Exercício de Atividade Remunerada (EAR), e disponibilidade de horário para viagens.

A empresa também exige experiência comprovada de no mínimo 12 meses na condução de bitrem, tritem, carreta, rodotrem ou ônibus interestadual, além de curso de movimentação de cargas indivisíveis.

As inscrições podem ser feitas pela internet, no site da empresa . Os interessados também podem comparecer presencialmente ao polo da JSL na Rua Colômbia, nº 975, no bairro Jardim das Nações, munidos de currículo atualizado e documento de identidade com foto (RG) para participar da entrevista.

Outras cidades do interior também estão vagas abertas. Os Postos de Atendimento ao Trabalhador (PAT) e secretarias de desenvolvimento econômico de Bauru , Marília , Botucatu e Ourinhos (SP) oferecem centenas de vagas de emprego para diversas áreas e níveis de escolaridade.

Para concorrer a qualquer uma das oportunidades, os interessados devem comparecer às unidades com RG, CPF, carteira de trabalho (física ou digital) e comprovante de endereço atualizado, ou realizar o cadastro nos canais oficiais de atendimento de cada município.

articles.standfirst: Prazo para inscrição no vestibular e parte dos cursos técnicos termina em 22 de outubro. Vagas são para campi em todo o estado e incluem também educação de jovens e adultos
articles.summary: Vagas são para campi em todo o estado.
articles.body:
O Instituto Federal de Santa Catarina (IFSC) abriu inscrições para mais de 5 mil vagas gratuitas para o Vestibular 2027/1, cursos técnicos e Educação de Jovens e Adultos com o ensino técnico (Proeja) .

O prazo para se inscrever para o vestibular e parte dos cursos técnicos é 22 de outubro .

Há vagas para diferentes campi, em todas as regiões do estado ( mais informações abaixo ). Confira os editais:

O IFSC oferece 50% das suas vagas para estudantes que cursaram o ensino médio em escolas públicas brasileiras, por meio do Sistema de Cotas para Escolas Públicas. As demais vagas são oferecidas por ampla concorrência.

Dentro do Sistema de Cotas para Escolas Públicas há ainda cotas para candidatos de baixa renda, autodeclarados pretos, pardos e indígenas, quilombolas e pessoas com deficiência.

IFSC Campus Florianópolis — Foto: IFSC/Divulgação

A taxa de inscrição para o Vestibular 2027/1 do IFSC é de R$ 95 .

São mais de 1,1 mil vagas distribuídas nos seguintes campi ( leia a lista de cursos mais abaixo ):

A prova será em 22 de novembro , das 14h às 18h30, com questões objetivas e redação.

A divulgação do resultado do vestibular está prevista para 17 de dezembro .

Cursos técnicos e Proeja são oferecidos em 22 campi

As aulas iniciam no primeiro semestre de 2027.

➡️ São mais de 4,2 mil vagas ofertadas em quatro tipos de curso :

ensino médio técnico (integrado) - para quem quer cursar o ensino médio junto com um curso técnico

técnicos subsequentes - para quem já concluiu o ensino médio

técnicos concomitantes - ensino técnico no IFSC e regular em outra escola

Proeja - Educação de Jovens e Adultos com o ensino técnico

➡️ Serão realizadas três formas de ingresso :

prova - exame com 28 questões de múltipla escolha e taxa de inscrição de R$ 70. A prova será em 29 de novembro

sorteio público - gratuito. Todos os inscritos são sorteados eletronicamente

por ordem de inscrição - gratuito. As vagas são preenchidas conforme a ordem em que os candidatos se inscrevem.

➡️ As datas de encerramento de inscrição variam conforme o tipo de seleção:

até 22 de outubro para os cursos com seleção por prova

articles.title: Estônia acusa Rússia de ataque incendiário; Kremlin nega | G1
articles.standfirst: Incidente ocorreu em agosto em prédio de empresa de defesa estoniana que fornece veículos de guerra à Ucrânia, segundo o governo báltico. Governo Putin chamou acusação de 'infundada'.
articles.summary: Incidente ocorreu em agosto em prédio de empresa de defesa estoniana que fornece veículos de guerra à Ucrânia, segundo o governo báltico. Governo Putin chamou acusação de 'infundada'.
articles.body:
Prédio da Milrem Robotics, empresa de defesa estoniana, em Tallin, capital da Estônia. Foto de maio de 2024. — Foto: Divulgação/Milrem Robotics

A Estônia acusou nesta terça-feira (29) a Rússia de estar por trás de um ataque incendiário contra uma empresa de defesa ocorrido em seu território em agosto.

O primeiro-ministro estoniano, Kristen Michal, disse que o Serviço de Segurança Interna da Estônia (KAPO) concluiu após investigação que um incêndio na empresa de defesa estoniana Milrem Robotics foi provocado por um ataque incendiário encomendado pelos serviços de segurança russos.

A empresa fornece veículos terrestres não tripulados para a Ucrânia em meio à guerra contra a Rússia, segundo o país báltico. O incêndio ocorreu na madrugada de 15 de agosto.

A Estônia não divulgou quais evidências utilizou para embasar a acusação, citando o caráter confidencial das informações dos serviços de segurança, mas afirmou que o incidente era consistente com outros atos de sabotagem realizados em nome da Rússia na Europa.

Minutos depois, o Kremlin negou envolvimento com o incidente e chamou a acusação estoniana de "infundada".

"Tais declarações são infundadas, mal pensadas, não têm absolutamente nenhuma relação com a realidade e carecem de qualquer tipo de raciocínio. Portanto, não podemos e não iremos levar tais declarações a sério", disse o porta-voz do Kremlin, Dmitry Peskov, a repórteres em coletiva nesta terça.

A acusação desta terça lembra uma outra feita, também de forma retroativa, pela Alemanha no início do mês, quando Berlim afirmou que a Rússia era responsável por um incidente envolvendo um drone carregado com explosivos no aeroporto de Leipzig.

O anúncio da Estônia também se junta a outras dezenas de outros incidentes híbridos —quando o ataque ou incidente não se encaixa com uma agressão bélica convencional— que têm ocorrido pela Europa nos últimos meses e pelo qual a Europa tem acusado a Rússia de estar por trás.

UE expressa apoio, e Otan diz que campanha russa de sabotagem russa não está funcionando

Após a denúncia, a Comissão Europeia expressou "solidariedade total" com a Estônia e chamou o incidente de "ataque inconsequente" russo.

O secretário-geral da Otan, Mark Rutte, afirmou nesta terça-feira (29) que a campanha de sabotagem e interferência da Rússia na Europa não está conseguindo minar o apoio europeu à Ucrânia.

"A Rússia continua sua campanha imprudente de ações hostis contra os aliados da Otan. Ela está tentando enfraquecer nossa determinação e interromper nosso apoio à Ucrânia. Mas a Rússia está fracassando, tanto no campo de batalha na Ucrânia quanto em minar nossa unidade e nosso apoio à Ucrânia", disse Rutte a jornalistas.

O presidente da França, Emmanuel Macron, chamou o incidente na Estônia de "escalada perigosa" e afirmou que a Rússia não conseguirá quebrar a união do bloco europeu.

O primeiro-ministro sueco, Ulf Kristersson, disse que o caso era "extremamente grave" e que a Suécia apoiava integralmente o país báltico.

articles.title: UNGA 81: Five key takeaways from general debate
articles.summary: The 81st United Nations General Assembly ends with AI, Palestine and wars dominating speeches.
articles.body:
The 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) concluded on Monday with artificial intelligence (AI), the Israel-Palestine conflict and the US-Israel war on Iran dominating world leaders’ addresses during the general debate.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, in his final address before his term ends, warned that the future of the world would be shaped by four tests: AI, climate change, wars and inequality.

“Across all four tests, the decisive issue is power. Power over force, money, energy, technology, rules and the future. That is why the UN Charter – and the work of the United Nations – matter more than ever,” Guterres said.

Speeches ranged from calls to reform the UN to appeals for upholding international law, as the global body has been undermined by the unilateral foreign policy pushed by United States President Donald Trump.

Here are the biggest takeaways from this year’s summit:

The situation in Palestine was a key issue among members amid Israel’s ongoing genocidal war on Gaza despite the so-called “ceasefire” and escalating settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank.

France, Canada, Iraq, the United Kingdom and others called for Palestinian sovereignty during their speeches.

“What credibility do we have if we continue to remain inactive in the face of Gaza,” French President Emmanuel Macron said in his address.

“Some boast of a supposed peace, but this peace hasn’t reopened humanitarian routes for a single second,” he said, adding: “Must we stand by and watch this spectacle that shames us all?”

Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, his Canadian counterpart Mark Carney and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud chaired a meeting at the UNGA on Palestinian statehood, which is being actively undermined by Israel. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has accelerated construction of illegal settlements and provided impunity to settlers in the occupied territory.

At the same time, the US-led Board of Peace unveiled a 66-project reconstruction blueprint with proposed funding of $2.4bn for the Gaza Strip on the sidelines of the UNGA.

However, the board’s plan excludes the UN agency for Palestinian refugees ( UNRWA ), saying it has no role in the future of Gaza. The decision was described by Palestinian political analyst and playwright Ahmed Najar to Al Jazeera as aligned with Israeli efforts to “marginalise and ultimately dismantle the agency, removing it not only from Gaza’s present but from its future”.

Dozens of delegates left the hall in protest as Netanyahu delivered his speech, in which he declared that Israeli forces would continue fighting against Hamas and Iran.

Trump defends military action on Venezuela, Iran

In his address, Trump emphasised that while others spoke of peace, he “made peace”.

Trump defended his actions in abducting the then-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January and said, since his military operation, hundreds of political prisoners had been freed in the South American country and that Caracas had signed the largest oil deal in history last month, covering “65 billion barrels of oil, which will benefit both Venezuela and the United States enormously and help drive down the cost of energy all over the world”.

“It was perhaps the biggest deal ever made. To the victor belong the spoils – you’ve all heard that,” Trump boasted.

Trump reiterated that he would never allow Tehran to have nuclear weapons and that the 12-day war in July 2025 had “obliterated their nuclear programme beneath mountains of rubble” as the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran had sunk “159 ships of their navy” to the bottom of the sea.

“I have a big decision to make – will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before … or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again,” he said, adding: “I believe we make a deal right after the elections.”

During sideline talks and one-on-one meetings, Iranian officials were in demand.

In his speech to delegates, President Masoud Pezeshkian emphasised that Iran had only “defended ourselves” amid attacks on his country and killings of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, scientists and children.

“We are not terrorists, our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country,” he said.

Pezeshkian added Iran would not accept that peaceful nuclear technology is held exclusively in the hands of a few countries.

“We will not bow our head and give up the right that is inherently ours,” he said.

Meanwhile, on the sidelines of the summit, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met his counterparts from India, Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan, Ukraine and other countries.

He also met US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner in a four-hour meeting mediated by Qatar.

World leaders used their time at the podium to call for a global approach to using AI as interest in the technology grows, but fears that it could escalate if unchecked are also growing.

In his address, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said AI was the “most consequential technology in the history of mankind”.

“It will impact science, the economy, politics, security, and the very essence of our humanity. Humans can and should be in the driver’s seat. We have a choice: we can compete, cooperate or slow down. For me, cooperation is the best way forward,” he said.

While discussions are moving away from a good-versus-bad dichotomy, officials disagreed on approaches.

While Guterres and the European Union called for safety standards and international rules, Trump said AI innovation should not be constrained by international regulation, adding that the US should control its AI sector.

Chinese President Xi Jinping skipped the UNGA despite being in the US for a summit with Trump. He sent Vice President Han Zheng to attend.

Xi rarely attends the UNGA. He had sent Premier Li Qiang in his place last year. In 2024, Foreign Minister Wang Yi attended the annual gathering.

Without mentioning Iran in his address, Han reiterated Beijing’s position that “sovereignty and security of countries in the Middle East, including the Gulf, should be respected”.

“China calls for advancing the governance of the West Bank and the post-conflict reconstruction of Gaza in accordance with the principle of the Palestinians governing Palestine. It also calls for bringing the Palestinian question back onto the right track of the two-state solution at an early date,” he said.

Han also called for a “people-centred approach and develop AI for the positive and for good, narrow the digital divide, and promote development that is universally beneficial”.

articles.title: In 1965, an artist proposed restoring Manhattan’s lost native woods on one street corner; by 1998, the small pre-colonial forest had become a protected city landmark
articles.summary: Explore Time Landscape in Lower Manhattan, a unique urban woodland created by artist Alan Sonfist, preserving the area's pre-colonial heritage and ecology.
articles.body: In Lower Manhattan, most people who pass the corner of LaGuardia Place and West Houston Street only look at it from the pavement. It is an enclosed patch of tall trees and thick undergrowth, with no lawn or benches, wedged between academic buildings, cafes and traffic. It is easy to mistake it for an abandoned lot, and that is part of its charm.It is actually a constructed woodland named Time Landscape. Artist Alan Sonfist proposed the idea in 1965, according to NYC Parks. After studying New York's flora, geology and history, he and local community members planted a 200 by 40 foot plot in 1978 with native trees, shrubs, wild grasses, flowers, rocks and earth. In 1998 the city commemorated it with an official historical marker, treating it as a living piece of the island's heritage.An empty block and a great ideaThe site was available for an unusual reason. In the 1950s, the tenements and townhomes on the east side of LaGuardia Place were condemned and demolished for a roadway that community protest later halted. The block sat vacant for decades. Sonfist, born in 1946, first brought the idea to the city at 19, approaching the mayor, the Museum of Modern Art, the Metropolitan Museum and the Parks department. He imagined it as one of several recreated landscapes for the city. That one corner became one of the first pieces of environmental art in an American city, and it helped establish the idea that nature could be treated as a public monument.The thirteen years between 1965 and 1978 were not wasted. There was research and negotiation over many years, and the work involved local people as well as scientists. The planting finally went in under Mayor Ed Koch in 1978. The result is less garden and more a carefully curated reproduction.Reading the land before the cityTo build a forest that might have stood there, Sonfist had first to figure out what the area had looked like. Greenwich Village was previously marshland with sandy hills called Sapokanican by the Canarsie people and Zantberg by the Dutch. To the west ran Minetta Brook, full of trout, and the area was a favourite spot for fishing and duck hunting. Over the following three and a half centuries, farms, homes, shops and factories replaced the marshland, and NYC Parks describes Time Landscape as a natural landmark of the seventeenth century and earlier.Later research has proved how rich that terrain was. The Wildlife Conservation Society worked ten years on the Mannahatta Project, reconstructing the streams, ponds, coastlines, hills and forests of Manhattan just before Henry Hudson arrived in 1609. This research continues today at the Welikia Project in the New York Botanical Garden, where visitors can explore an interactive map of the environment before the city. Time Landscape was a generation earlier but explores the same topic in living form.The planting also portrays three stages of forest growth, from grasses and flowers to saplings to mature trees. The southern end is the youngest stage, with red cedar trees and hazelnut shrubs dressed in wildflowers. The centre holds a small grove of beech, a tree native to the region, grown from saplings taken from a Bronx forest that Sonfist knew as a child, and it stands among red cedar, black cherry and witch hazel. The north end is a mature oak woodland with white ash and American elm scattered through it.Today the plot sits on city land assigned to the Department of Transportation and is maintained by Parks under its Greenstreets programme, with help from volunteers, according to the NYC Parks page. Parks describes the result as a slowly developing forest, so the plot keeps changing year by year. Readers who want to see the precolonial island for themselves can use the interactive Welikia map, which the New York Botanical Garden now maintains as the follow-up to the Mannahatta Project.You use AI every day. articles.title: US’s Marco Rubio says UK airbase incident involved ‘foreign actor’
articles.summary: Washington’s top diplomat calls the suspected plot ‘a very serious situation’ after five were arrested over the weekend.
articles.body:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said a “foreign actor” was involved in a suspected bomb plot near an airbase in the United Kingdom used by the US military.

Police arrested five men, all British nationals from London, in their early to mid-20s, on Sunday after being alerted by a local farmer about three white vans driving towards RAF Fairford, a British base that houses US bombers flying missions against Iran.

The counterterrorism police said on Monday they were investigating whether individuals were acting for a foreign state in an apparent plot to attack the airbase. They later said the suspects would be released on bail.

Commenting on the suspected plot and arrests on the Hannity programme on Fox News late on Monday, Rubio said, “What happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation.”

“It’s one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor. I won’t get into great detail about that yet,” he added.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had said in July the Fairford base was a legitimate target.

Iran’s embassy in London said in a statement on Monday it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” that it was involved, which it said would fuel “Iranophobia propaganda” in the UK.

Trump said on Sunday the UK and the US had had the suspects “under investigation” for a while and alleged, “They were looking to do big damage to our fort.”

After hearing news that suspects were being released on bail, Trump said on Monday the case “might be” linked to Iran but declined to elaborate.

The UK gave the US permission in March to use Fairford for “specific defensive operations into Iran” to destroy Iranian missiles at source.

US bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing at the base – the only one on the British mainland used for this purpose.

Residents in the rural Cotswolds area surrounding Fairford said the site, which hosts a range of US military equipment and personnel, had seen increased activity and security in recent months.

Authorities evacuated about 85 households from a nearby village early on Sunday, but they were allowed to return home the next day.

Tehran has previously warned London against allowing its bases to be used by the US in operations against Iran.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has accused London of “putting British lives in danger” by allowing the bases to be used “for aggression against Iran”.

articles.title: 'First' in 200 years: US woman who killed classmate at 18 faces execution at 50
articles.summary: Christa Pike was 18 when she was convicted of killing her 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995.
articles.body: Christa Pike was 18 when she was convicted of killing her 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995. Now 50, Pike is scheduled to be executed in Tennessee on Wednesday, in what would be the state's first execution of a woman in 200 years.Pike and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, were students at Knoxville Job Corps when Slemmer was killed. Prosecutors said Pike believed Slemmer was a romantic rival and lured her to an isolated area, where she and Shipp tortured and killed her.The case drew national attention because of the brutality of the killing and the ages of those involved. Shipp later admitted that he carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satanism, into Slemmer's body.Pike has never denied that she killed Slemmer. However, her lawyers and supporters argue that she should not be executed for a crime committed when she was 18, citing her untreated mental illness and a childhood marked by severe abuse and neglect.Tennessee Governor Bill Lee announced on Monday that he would not grant Pike clemency. Her lawyers have now asked the US Supreme Court to stop the execution.Lawyers cite abuse and mental illnessPike's lawyers say she suffered years of sexual abuse and neglect as a child. Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell said she was sexually abused from toddlerhood and raped at ages 11 and 17.He also argued that lawyers who represented Pike during the sentencing phase of her trial failed to present the jury with important details about her childhood or make her age a significant part of their case.Pike was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. She told police that she had initially intended only to fight Slemmer but that the confrontation escalated into a frenzied attack.In her clemency petition, her lawyers said her untreated mental illness and traumatic upbringing left her unable to "put the brakes on."“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in a statement included in her clemency petition.Ferrell said research into adolescent brain development has advanced since Pike's trial and argued that her death sentence is an outlier.Shipp, who was 17 when Slemmer was killed, received a life sentence with the possibility of parole because of his age. He was denied parole last year. A third teenager who admitted to being an accessory received probation.Ferrell said other people in Tennessee who were sentenced to death for crimes committed at 18 have since had their sentences reduced.The Death Penalty Information Center says 275 people have been executed in the US during the modern death penalty era for crimes committed at ages 18, 19 or 20. It also says death sentences for people in that age group have become increasingly uncommon.“If Christa Pike was tried today, I do not believe a jury that knew about the documented sexual abuse and neglect she experienced as a child would sentence her to death,” Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said.Slemmer's mother wants execution to go aheadSlemmer's mother, May Martinez, has spent decades waiting for her daughter's case to reach this point. She supports Pike's execution and has said her daughter never had the opportunity to grow up.“Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run,” Martinez said.Martinez said Slemmer volunteered with the Special Olympics, enjoyed roller skating and hoped to work in computers.“She was easygoing. She was a computer geek to begin with. She and my husband would build and tear apart the computers constantly,” Martinez said. “She trusted everybody, and that was her downfall.”Martinez recalled speaking to her daughter by telephone from Job Corps on the night of the killing. The call kept dropping because of poor reception, and by the time Martinez called back, Slemmer had already left.“Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst. Colleen’s birthday was last week. She would have been 51,” Martinez said.Prosecutors said Pike attacked Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large piece of asphalt. The presence of the pentagram became part of the wider attention surrounding the case during the period of widespread fears about Satanism known as the "satanic panic" of the 1980s and 1990s.A rare execution of a womanIf Pike's execution goes ahead, it would be Tennessee's first execution of a woman since 1820, according to Maher.Executions of women are also uncommon across the US. Since 1976, 18 women have been executed in the country, accounting for about 1% of all executions, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.Missouri executed Amber McLaughlin in 2023 for a 2003 killing. McLaughlin, a transgender woman, is believed to have been the first transgender woman executed in the US.The federal government executed Lisa Montgomery in 2021, marking the first federal execution of a woman in nearly seven decades. Georgia executed a female inmate in 2015.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Lebanese are watching Israel’s upcoming election, but few expect change
articles.summary: Lebanese are anticipating continued Israeli aggression in Lebanon after the election.
articles.body:
Nabatieh, Lebanon: A pushcart that Hadi Nasrallah uses to sell fresh orange juice is all this Khiam resident has left to his name.

His home was destroyed by the Israeli bombing, while his village is among the dozens across southern Lebanon currently occupied by Israel.

In a few weeks, Israelis will head to the polls to elect a new government. But Nasrallah, like so many others Al Jazeera spoke to, expects little to change even if Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – who launched the war on Lebanon in 2023 – is defeated in October’s general election.

“Israel has territorial ambitions. It is about Greater Israel. That is why whoever wins in the election won’t stop the destructive military policies and leave southern Lebanon,” Nasrallah told Al Jazeera. “All this talk about creating security is a cover for their true intentions.”

Israel has been the enemy for many in southern Lebanon for decades. But over the past three years, under Netanyahu’s leadership, periodic clashes between the Israeli military and Hezbollah have transformed into an intense and sustained war.

The Israeli military says it is only against Hezbollah. But its attacks have rampantly targeted civilian areas, killing at least 8,920 people and injuring 30,595 others since October 2023. Almost 6 percent of Lebanese territory, along the border with Israel, remains occupied – all in the name of security.

Now, Netanyahu is fighting for his political survival. However, Netanyahu’s government is not the only political force in the country that supports military operations beyond Israel’s borders.

Netanyahu’s main political challenger, Gadi Eisenkot – head of the Yashar party and former army chief of staff – is also projecting an image as a security hawk.

He is known in Lebanon for formulating a military strategy – the so-called Dahiyeh Doctrine – during Israel’s war with Hezbollah in 2006. It calls for the use of massive force in military operations, even against civilian infrastructure, as a deterrent against its enemies. This strategy has been deployed in Israel’s recent wars, particularly in its devastating aerial assaults on Beirut’s southern suburbs.

Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, insists on freedom of action for Israel’s military. But he accused Netanyahu of bowing to US pressure to halt operations in Beirut, with no major attacks on the Lebanese capital since April. He also insists that the military should be able to attack Hezbollah anywhere in Lebanon.

He has also accused the prime minister of running the war “blindly, arrogantly, and irresponsibly” and using military force without any achievable political goals or a sustainable diplomatic horizon to back Israel’s military actions.

But Netanyahu and Eisenkot’s stated goals are essentially the same – a demilitarised southern Lebanon, the disarmament of Hezbollah and long-term “security” for the residents of northern Israel.

“They are all the same,” Marcella Nasreddine, a resident of Beirut’s southern suburbs, told Al Jazeera. “It has been the same policy since 1948 … destroy and control … Israel wants to control more territory.”

Across the Lebanese border, in southern Syria, many are increasingly concerned about the Israeli military push into hundreds of square kilometres of Syrian land. The current Israeli leadership says the military is not leaving. Eisenkot does not appear to want to rush a withdrawal and appears to intend to use the occupation as leverage against the new Syrian government.

It has left people on both sides of the Lebanon-Syria border concerned that instead of bringing change, Israel’s upcoming elections could make their situation worse.

“I think you should focus on what happens from now until the elections rather than who will lead Israel,” Ali Jarmak, a resident of the southern city of Nabatieh, told Al Jazeera. “Netanyahu is not leading in the polls, so he may resort to escalating the war here to gain more votes.”

Netanyahu has already delayed the diplomatic track with the Lebanese government. There have been no negotiations between Israeli and Lebanese officials since early August. Israel is also refusing further withdrawals from Lebanon until Hezbollah fully disarms. But Hezbollah is refusing to do so and threatening to confront any attempt by the government to disarm the group.

Prime Minister Nawaf Salam is under pressure to extend the state’s authority across Lebanon. He told the United Nations General Assembly last week that the framework agreement signed with Israel must be translated into practical steps, under a clear timetable, with a verification mechanism to ensure all its provisions are carried out.

It fell on deaf ears. Instead, the Israeli military has been stepping up attacks on southern Lebanon, and the army command is discussing “a new phase in operations”. The debate among Israel’s political rivals is not about maintaining dominance, but about how.

articles.title: In 1998, a Florida man mixed his father-in-law’s ashes into concrete and sank the first memorial reef off Sarasota; the idea grew into more than 2,500 living reefs across 25 U.S. coastal sites
articles.summary: Discover how a Florida man turned his father-in-law's ashes into a memorial reef, leading to over 2,500 living reefs across the U.S. that provide marine habitat.
articles.body: What began as an unusual request from a dying man became a new way to remember people while creating habitat beneath the sea. According to The Washington Post, the story began in 1998, when Don Brawley incorporated his father-in-law Carleton “Petey” Palmer’s cremated remains into a concrete artificial reef. The memorial reef was cast in Sarasota, Florida, and later placed on the Gulf of Mexico floor. Palmer’s request eventually led to Eternal Reefs, which has deployed thousands of memorial reefs at permitted sites along the US coast. By 2023, Eternal Reefs reported that more than 2,500 memorial reefs had been placed at about 25 locations.An unusual request becomes a new kind of memorialThe story began with an artificial-reef project rather than a funeral service. According to Eternal Reefs, Don Brawley and Todd Barber were college roommates who often dived in the Florida Keys and became concerned about the deterioration they saw on the reefs. They began looking for a way to recreate marine habitat and eventually developed Reef Balls, hollow concrete structures with textured surfaces designed to provide places where marine organisms could settle and grow. The Reef Ball Development Group and Reef Ball Foundation went on to develop and deploy these structures as artificial reefs in different locations.The idea of turning a reef ball into a memorial came from a much more personal request. In 1998, Brawley’s father-in-law, Carleton “Petey” Palmer, told him that he wanted his cremated remains to become part of a reef. When Palmer died, Brawley remembered what he had asked for and decided to make it happen. Palmer’s cremated remains were mixed into the concrete used to make a reef ball that was to be placed in the sea near Sarasota, Florida.On May 1, 1998, ten Nautilus and 20 Aquarius reef balls were cast, including the one containing Palmer’s remains. Once placed on the ocean floor, it became what Eternal Reefs describes as its first memorial reef. Rather than simply marking a final resting place, the structure was intended to become part of the underwater environment, providing a surface where marine organisms could settle and grow. What began as one man’s unusual final wish eventually became the idea behind a new kind of underwater memorial.How ashes become an artificial reefEternal Reefs' process involves mixing cremated remains directly into marine concrete to form a reef memorial structure. Families can take part in creating the memorial by mixing the ashes into the wet concrete and adding handprints, notes, or other environmentally friendly items. The finished memorial is then allowed to cure before being deployed at an approved marine location. According to Eternal Reefs, its memorials are placed at public reef sites established for recreational activities such as fishing and diving.Design plays a crucial role in the functioning of the memorial beneath water. The reef balls have holes that let water pass through them, and their textured surface gives marine species a place to attach. Over time, algae, invertebrates, and other marine creatures colonise the structure, while fish use the holes inside and around it. This does not mean the structure becomes a coral reef in the strict sense. This is an artificial reef meant to provide additional habitat. The structure’s ecological value depends on its location and the marine ecosystem at the chosen site. The idea later expanded beyond individual memorials. Today, Eternal Reefs offers group deployments at permitted coastal locations, allowing several families to have reefs deployed in a single operation. The company’s schedule currently includes reefs in Florida and other coastal areas.From one family’s wish to thousands of reefsAfter Palmer’s reef was placed in the Gulf, other families began asking Brawley if they could do something similar for people they had lost. The idea offered a different way to remember someone. For some families, it was an alternative to keeping cremated remains in an urn or scattering them. For others, the appeal was that the memorial could also have a place in the sea, where it could eventually become part of the marine surroundings.More than 25 years after Palmer’s reef was created, the basic process remains much the same. Cremated remains are incorporated into a concrete reef structure, which is then placed at an approved marine site. Over time, marine organisms can settle on the structure and around it, making the memorial part of the underwater landscape. What started with one family’s request eventually opened the door for others who wanted to remember their loved ones in a place connected to the sea.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Hayden Panettiere’s ex Wladimir Klitschko petitions to protect their daughter’s inheritance
articles.summary: Actor Hayden Panettiere’s ex-fiancé Wladimir Klitschko has filed an urgent petition asking that he be allowed to act as their 11-year-old daughter’s temporary representative in California court to protect her inheritance after the death of her mother.
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — Actor Hayden Panettiere’s ex-fiancé Wladimir Klitschko has filed an urgent petition asking that he be allowed to act as their 11-year-old daughter’s temporary representative in California court to protect her inheritance after the death of her mother. Klitschko, a Ukrainian former world champion boxer, has had full custody of the girl, Kaya, for most of her life, and she has lived with him in Ukraine. Kaya is Panettiere’s sole heir. The filing in a Los Angeles County court cites items seized in a federal investigation of the actor’s death, unnamed and unauthorized people accessing her residence in Los Angeles, and valuables that are missing. The petition says it is “urgent and essential” that Klitschko be granted the legal status of temporary guardian of his daughter’s estate. “Without an immediate appointment for these purposes, there is a high probability that property belonging to Hayden’s Estate may be lost, damaged or dissipated before a duly appointed personal representative can be in place to protect it,” the filing says. Klitschko’s lawyers filed the petition on Thursday, but it did not become publicly known until Monday, when it was reported by TMZ. The filing emphasizes that his intention is solely to protect his daughter’s future assets until a permanent administrator can be put in place. Panettiere, the former star of the TV series “Heroes” and “Nashville,” died Aug. 16 at age 36. A coroner’s report obtained by The Associated Press said her death was from an accidental overdose of several drugs, including fentanyl, and she had been in rehab just weeks before. She was found unresponsive in an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina. The petition says that federal agents have taken Panettiere’s property in an investigation, and there is no authorized person to deal with them and assure it is returned. The filing says that before her death, Panettiere and Klitschko hired security to protect her home because an unnamed person had gained unauthorized access. The petition says it’s expected the same person will continue to try to “misappropriate” property belonging to her estate. A hearing on the issue is scheduled for Oct. 8. In her memoir released earlier this year, Panettiere acknowledged being addicted to alcohol and having postpartum depression after her daughter’s birth in 2014. Kaya went to live with Klitschko full-time when she was 2. Panettiere’s father told investigators that when she died she had plans to visit her daughter in Ukraine days later. Klitschko, 50, an Olympic gold medalist, held several heavyweight titles between 2000 and 2015. He and Panettiere began dating in 2009 and got engaged in 2013. His older brother Vitali, also a former champion boxer, is mayor of Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital. The two brothers, sons of a Soviet major general, have worked to protect their country during its war with Russia.

articles.title: Palestine weekly: Israeli politicians vie to look toughest before election
articles.summary: With Israelis voting on October 27, ministers are staging illegal settlement launches as campaign events.
articles.body:
The final stretch before Israel’s election is unfolding in an increasingly charged political atmosphere, with parties and candidates keenly aware of how every move will play with voters.

This week, ministers launched an illegal West Bank settlement at a ceremony that doubled as a stump speech, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defiantly addressed the United Nations General Assembly as delegations walked out.

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir released another video from an Israeli prison, this time filming himself threatening to kill jailed Hamas figure Hassan Salameh. Meanwhile, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for the army to “go to war” in the occupied West Bank.

All of this unfolded as the Jewish festival of Sukkot arrived, bringing closures and incursions at Al-Aqsa Mosque.

Settlement openings, demolitions and holiday closures

On September 23, Israeli ministers and members of parliament attended the founding ceremony of the new illegal settlement in the occupied West Bank, Metzoke Eretz, Haaretz reported. The politicians, including Smotrich, argued that only a Netanyahu-led government would sustain the momentum of settlement building.

The site had previously been the Netzah Harel outpost, established in 2023, in the vicinity of the now-ethnically cleansed Bedouin community of al-Muarrajat al-Wasat, on private Palestinian land. Metzoke Eretz is one of 104 settlements the Israeli government has legalised – even if they remain illegal under international law – during its term.

Demolitions continued alongside the settlement building, focused on Masafer Yatta, a Palestinian community in the southern occupied West Bank, which has seen a large number of large-scale demolitions in recent weeks. Israeli forces razed 24 homes in the village of Jinba on September 23, displacing about 180 people, more than 80 of them children, according to Israeli rights group B’Tselem.

Meanwhile, after days of road closures for Palestinians across the occupied West Bank, on Sunday, Israeli authorities announced a weeklong closure of the territory and its crossings for the Jewish holidays.

Forces shut roads and village entrances around Ramallah, including those of Turmus Aya, Aboud, Nabi Saleh, Atara and Taybeh, and set up checkpoints at Yabrud, Ein Siniya and Jaba. Palestinian news agency Wafa described “severe and unprecedented” congestion that day, with hundreds of vehicles stranded at checkpoints.

On Monday, soldiers at Atara stopped ambulances from crossing, forcing residents to ferry patients through in private cars and hand them over at the checkpoint, according to field activists Ayed Jafry and Fidaa Barghouthi. Jafry also reported soldiers closing the gate at Sinjil, the town’s only entrance.

In occupied East Jerusalem, Palestinian movement was further curtailed to make way for settler worship. On September 24, the far-right rabbi Yehuda Glick led a group in religious rituals inside the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, which has since seen thousands of settlers enter it during the Jewish holidays.

Tensions were already high after a Palestinian allegedly drove into a group of Israelis at a checkpoint west of Ramallah on September 23, critically wounding Neria Leiter, the son of Israel’s ambassador to the United States, before being shot dead .

West Bank: Settlers stake out the groves

Israeli settlers uprooted olive trees in Beit Ur al-Fauqa, and Israeli bulldozers razed groves in Nabi Saleh and Beit Rima, destroying hundreds of trees, many of them centuries old, according to local activists.

Israeli authorities called the Nabi Saleh operation a security measure tied to a settler’s killing near the illegal settlement of Halamish on September 20, but activists noted that the grove is near neither the spring where the shooting occurred nor a settlement.

With the harvest approaching, settlers were seen and documented stealing olives in Sinjil, Turmus Aya, and Umm Safa on Monday, according to Wafa.

Pogroms also continued, including in Farkha, where dozens of settlers, some carrying military-issue rifles, beat two men on September 24. On Sunday, settlers beat two men in Burqa and attacked the Kaabneh community near Taybeh, cutting off its water and electricity, Wafa reported.

Gaza: Killings continue under ‘ceasefire’

In the Gaza Strip, meanwhile, daily killings continued amid drone strikes on people’s homes and displacement camps.

The week’s dead, according to local reports and activist accounts, include Jabr Muqbil, 34, an exchange-office owner killed in Deir el-Balah on September 24, when relatives who rushed to the scene were wounded in a follow-up strike. Israel claimed Muqbil was a Hamas member.

Separately, on September 23, Osama Abu Khater and Mohammad Abu Elwan were killed in an al-Mawasi drone strike, with Israel describing the latter as a Hamas finance official.

On Saturday, 12-year-old Muhammad Sief al-Din al-Shakhrit was reported killed in the al-Mawasi area. And on Sunday, Oday Adli al-Assar, 28, was killed in a drone strike in Khan Younis.

Then, on September 28, a strike on the roof of a home sheltering displaced people in Gaza City’s al-Mashahara area killed Amal Khalid al-Ajla and wounded others.

Conditions in the beleaguered Strip continue to deteriorate, with Israel still preventing aid from entering in sufficient amounts. A UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) report this week found 92 percent of Gaza’s economic establishments damaged or destroyed.

The US-created Board of Peace had said it would not work with UNRWA , the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, in Gaza. And while the board’s envoy, Nickolay Mladenov, announced a $2.45bn reconstruction package for the Strip, he tied its full implementation to Hamas disarmament.

Over the course of the week, Gaza’s Ministry of Health recorded another 27 Palestinians killed, reaching a post-“ceasefire” death toll of 1,421. The number of Palestinians killed since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023 passed the 74,000 mark, reaching 74,022 as of September 28.

articles.title: Fat dogs of Delhi: The unusual election gripping the Indian capital
articles.summary: The contest to crown the Indian capital's "chonkiest" dog has attracted thousands of votes.
articles.body:
An unusual election has gripped India's capital, drawing thousands of voters and enthusiastic campaigners to crown Delhi's "chonkiest" dog.

The knockout competition began after Fat Dogs of Delhi, an Instagram page dedicated to the city's more generously proportioned canines, invited people to nominate their favourite neighbourhood dogs.

But what started as a joke quickly turned competitive, with supporters creating campaign posters, endorsement videos and memes to drum up votes for their favourites.

The contest has attracted thousands of votes and tens of thousands of new followers on Instagram as it approaches its grand finale on Wednesday after several rounds of intense online voting.

Many of the contestants do not have a single owner. Instead, they are neighbourhood fixtures, living on the city's streets and cared for by networks of residents, shopkeepers and workers who feed them, give them names and keep an eye on their health.

Two of the dogs taking part died while the tournament was under way, prompting tributes from people who had been following and voting for them.

The person behind the page, who asked to remain anonymous, told the BBC the idea came after seeing people on X run similar knockout contests.

"Why not do it as a fun little thing for people to bond over?" she said.

The first 64 nominations were accepted - and the names were almost as colourful as the candidates themselves.

There is Dahi Bhalli, named after a popular north Indian street food of soft savoury donut soaked in yoghurt and tamarind sauce. Mahakutteshwar is a play on names associated with deities and temples, incorporating the Hindi word kutta, or dog. Others include Googoo, Rambabu and the formidably named Kutta Singh - literally, "Dog Singh".

In the first round, the 64 contestants were divided into 32 groups and voters had to choose one from each. The 32 who won progressed to the next step and the losers were knocked out.

Similar elimination rounds were held and on Tuesday only eight remained in the final race for the crown.

Since the contest began, supporters have been picking sides, producing their own campaign material, from elaborate posters to reels and memes, and approaching friends and strangers for votes. And the enthusiasm has spread well beyond Delhi, with supporters as far away as Kerala and Kolkata picking favourites and campaigning on their behalf.

The scale of the response has caught the organiser off guard.

"I did not expect it to blow up to this extent for sure," she told the BBC, adding that her account has gained thousands of followers. "I love the sense of community that we have right now."

But the competition has also faced criticism from some social media users, who have questioned whether it risks celebrating obesity in dogs.

Being overweight can contribute to a range of health problems in dogs and can shorten their lives. Some critics have also raised concerns that celebrating the animals for their size could normalise overfeeding.

Meanwhile, the finalists continue to generate excitement, with a line-up as quirky as the competition itself.

Googoo is a 46kg (101lb) mixed-breed who is staying at an animal-care centre in Delhi where, somewhat ironically, he is trying to lose weight.

His meals are being regulated and he undergoes regular medical checks. The teenager who entered Googoo in the competition told The Indian Express newspaper that he first spotted him in a local park in 2021, when the dog was less than half his current size.

Googoo's supporters have since produced posters and social media campaigns urging people to vote for him, with some declaring him the "GOAT" - or greatest of all time.

The organisers now hope the contest's unexpected popularity can be channelled into helping stray animals. She said the page had begun highlighting animal-welfare groups and individuals seeking donations.

The light-hearted contest comes at a time when the presence and management of community dogs is the subject of a much more serious debate in the capital.

Delhi's stray dog population is estimated at one million, with suburban Noida, Ghaziabad and Gurugram also seeing a population rise, municipal sources say.

In many neighbourhoods, they are treated almost as community pets, fed by residents and cared for, while in others they are a source of fear, particularly because of dog bites, aggressive packs and the risk of rabies.

Last year, India's top court ordered strays in Delhi and its suburbs to be moved to animal shelters amid concerns over rising "menace of dog bites leading to rabies" - sparking outrage among animal-lovers and activists.

The order was later modified to allow sterilised and vaccinated dogs to be returned to their localities.

Many of those campaigning for the dogs say the contest has put the focus on the more affectionate side of Delhi's relationship with the animals.

For the final, the organisers plan to set up ballot boxes at three locations across Delhi, staffed by volunteers, allowing people to vote for their favourite dog in person as well as online.

After weeks of campaigning and thousands of votes, Delhi will then have its winner - who will officially be its "chonkiest" dog.

articles.body: In today’s newsletter: Three NBC News reporters hit the road for a six-day trip to discover what’s on voters’ minds. The attorney for a former Cornell University student says law enforcement and the school failed to protect her after she raised allegations of sexual assault. And Jack Smith faces questions on his handling of the investigation into Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election results. Here’s what to know today. Drive to Decision Day: What voters are most concerned about heading into midterms Americans are frustrated with the direction the country is headed as the midterm elections approach — an atmosphere that typically blows up on the party in power. They’re angry about rising prices, ballooning interest rates and foreign wars. They are afraid that AI will automate many jobs while driving up utility prices. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. So, NBC News took a road trip — over the course of six days and eight stops, three reporters hit some of the most competitive congressional districts to find out what’s driving people’s votes ahead of November. This “Drive to Decision Day” covered one-third of the most closely contested House races in the nation and two key Senate races. Read the full story about our August road trip and watch the NBC News Reports documentary. More election news: The Data Dive: Steve Kornacki explains what’s at stake in a crucial Iowa Senate battleground race. Cornell rape accuser’s attorney says the school and law enforcement failed a young woman The attorney representing a former Cornell University student who said she was raped in 2024 and pressured to take ketamine, accused law enforcement and the school of failing his client. The former student alleges that Chi Phi fraternity brothers sexually assaulted her and that one sent a message encouraging other members to participate in the attack. The fraternity chapter was subsequently barred from campus, but no one was criminally charged. Thomas P. Giuffra says his client went to the university’s police department after the alleged attack but did not speak with anyone beyond the first person who took her report. Officers failed to follow up on key pieces of evidence, including the group chat. Cornell has pushed back on the suggestion that those involved in the incident faced few consequences at the time, saying the Title IX proceedings resulted in a range of sanctions, including expulsions and suspensions. The civil suit has prompted Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten to reopen the case and consider whether to bring charges related to the allegations. He promised to pursue any new evidence “zealously.” Read the full story here. Senate GOP to press Jack Smith on Trump Jan. 6 probe as DOJ targets investigators Former special counsel Jack Smith will testify today before the Senate Judiciary Committee about his handling of the investigation into Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election results leading up to the Jan. 6 attacks. Smith has said he believes a jury would have convicted Trump in the election case had it gone to trial and dismissed notions he was “influenced or directed by the Biden administration.” Smith, along with other FBI and Justice Department officials, has faced criticism by the president’s allies in the Senate over involvement in past Trump investigations. Last year, the administration launched a so-called grand conspiracy investigation to examine actions taken by federal law enforcement individuals dating back to 2016, which would fall outside the typical five-year statute of limitations for most federal crimes. Read the full story here. Ahead of a rare execution, lone woman on Tennessee’s death row says “I am at peace” Tennessee is set to execute 50-year-old Christa Pike on Wednesday by lethal injection — the first time in more than 200 years that a state will put a woman to death, according to historical records. Knoxville police say in 1995, then 18-year-old Pike and others lured a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, to an abandoned steam plant, attacked her and fatally beat her. The case gained traction after investigators said it was tied to the occult because of a pentagram found carved in Slemmer’s chest. Pike’s lawyers have asked the Supreme Court to halt the execution, saying she suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder stemming from sexual abuse during her childhood. Tennessee corrections officials say they would try to fulfill certain requests made by Pike, including using female guards to transfer her and the use of an all-female execution team. Pike, who has been on the state’s death row for over three decades, doesn’t dispute her role in the killing. In a letter to NBC News, she said that she is at peace whether her clemency is granted, saying, “I am only nervous about the process.” Read the full story here. Staff Pick: Why lawmakers are scrambling to save a National Archives facility A family friend from the San Francisco Bay Area, where I grew up, asked if I had heard about the plan to shut down a National Archives facility there and move thousands of historical records important to the Asian American community out of California. It wasn’t on my radar. So during a recent trip, I sat down with Rep. Kevin Mullin, a Democrat who’s been leading the fight against the move, and a local genealogist who frequently does research there. They told me the facility houses old immigration, court and other records stored there from the 1898 Chinese Exclusion Act, Angel Island Immigration Station and the Japanese American incarceration during WWII. There are even documents from the Supreme Court’s landmark Wong Kim Ark decision, which established that a child born to foreign parents on U.S. soil is an American citizen. The National Archives and Records Administration has said the closure of this facility and others will reduce the agency’s real estate footprint and save money as it moves to digitize records. But opponents argue it’s critical that descendants of people who are in these records have access to them, and that many of these AAPI families still live nearby in the Bay Area or California. articles.body:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been jailed for seven years after being convicted of child sexual abuse.

Judge Lord Harrower said Dott robbed his victims of "a significant part of their childhood" and said his behaviour bore the hallmarks of grooming.

Dott had denied two charges of lewd and libidinous behaviour towards a girl and a boy between 1993 and 2010 but was found guilty following a trial at the High Court in Glasgow.

The 49-year-old Scot, who won the world snooker title in 2006, showed no emotion as he was sentenced, only nodding to someone in the public gallery as he was led away.

Lord Harrower told the High Court in Edinburgh that each of Dott's victims were vulnerable for reasons beyond their age.

He said Dott rewarded the victims with treats and disguised his abuse as being part of a game.

The former snooker champion was 16 or 17 when he abused the girl, who was about nine when her ordeal began.

Dott's abuse of the second victim - a boy aged about eight - began about 10 years later.

The court heard that he warned them they would not be believed if they told anyone about his actions.

The judge added Dott's victims had experienced "overwhelming emotions of fear, shame and anger" as a result of the abuse, affecting their mental health into adulthood.

Dott's behaviour towards the children "involved a gross violation of trust".

As Lord Harrower addressed him, Dott repeatedly shook his head in apparent disbelief.

The judge added social work reports have deemed Dott poses a "below average risk of reoffending", but as he still maintains his innocence, Lord Harrower could not take into account any remorse from Dott.

The court also heard that Dott has already been the subject of threats and has been moved within prison as a result.

Euan Dow, representing Dott, told the court the father-of-two was now separated from his wife but "continues to enjoy the support of his family and friends".

He added Dott suffers from "long-standing mental health issues" and that his personal and professional reputations had been destroyed.

The sentence of seven years has been backdated to 24 August, which is when the 49-year-old was remanded in custody.

He will spend the rest of his life on the sex offenders register.

Procurator Fiscal Faye Cook, of the Crown Office, said: "Graeme Dott achieved success and public admiration but, in private, he exploited the trust of two children to abuse and coerce them.

"Dott's criminal behaviour has been his downfall and he now faces the consequences of his actions."

She added that "justice has no time limit" and encouraged any victims of historical abuse to report it.

During the trial, the court heard that Dott had exposed himself and inappropriately touched a primary school girl in the 1990s and attacked a young boy between 2006 and 2010.

Dott called the allegations made against him "disgusting".

The girl, now a woman in her 40s, said Dott had "caressed" her bottom while giving her a piggyback and that, on another occasion, he had exposed himself to her.

On another occasion, she said Dott, of Glasgow, suggested she "take her trousers down" and lifted her top and began kissing her stomach after asking if she wanted to "play a guessing game".

The victim said Dott would kiss her, touch her inappropriately and carried out a sexual act that would, if committed now, amount to rape.

She said she recalled the "smell" of creams Dott used for a skin condition after he kissed her and that the actions left her "shocked and scared".

The court heard that Dott bought her a teddy bear with a love heart on it in the course of the abuse.

The woman gave a new statement to police in 2025.

During his evidence, Dott's male victim said the abuse began shortly after Dott defeated Peter Ebdon to win his sole world title at The Crucible in Sheffield in 2006.

The boy, now a man in his 20s, said he was about eight years old when Dott molested him in a shower at a home in South Lanarkshire.

He told the court that Dott "rewarded" him with crisps and fizzy drinks and once handed him a £50 note, only to accuse the boy of stealing it when his parents found out he had the money.

He also said he was abused in a car on a number of occasions and "inappropriately touched" while Dott played online poker.

Dott was convicted of lewd and libidinous practices, which refer to any sexual crimes against children committed prior to 1 December 2010.

The offence was abolished in 2009, but is still used for crimes carried out before then.

Following his conviction in August, the World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association said it had permanently revoked Dott's membership with immediate effect.

Dott was previously suspended from all professional snooker activities on 9 April 2025 pending the outcome of his trial.

He was subsequently relegated from the professional ranking list at the conclusion of the 2025/26 season.

Dott has two previous convictions for minor road traffic offences in 2013 and 2015.

articles.title: MTV VMAs: Taylor Swift dominates but do music videos matter?
articles.summary: Cinematographer Melissa Cofie says their purpose has evolved with the growth of platforms like TikTok.
articles.body:
We're far from the days of blockbuster music videos playing back-to-back on TV channels like MTV.

Catchy hooks and sleek dance routines now dominate social media feeds, each hoping to stop people in their tracks long enough for them to give a new song a chance.

The evolution of this landscape was cemented last year when MTV axed five music channels in the UK after almost 40 years of rolling footage.

But despite the broadcaster reacting to the changes in viewing habits, its Video Music Awards (VMAs) still appear to hold power over music A-listers.

Pop music heavyweights, including Taylor Swift, Madonna and Charli XCX, were among those who turned up on Sunday to accept prizes and deliver dramatic performances.

Cinematographer Melissa Cofie tells BBC Newsbeat that while these award shows "may seem very performative to others", they are "so important" to those in the music industry.

"The sleepless nights, the months, the weeks that it takes to put together a music video, it's almost as much work as you would put into a film itself," she says.

But do music videos still hold the same importance for fans as they once did?

Cofie, who has directed music videos, feels their purpose has evolved over the last couple of decades.

For her, they're more of a way to "connect with artists" and for them to express their vision, rather than a crucial part of their press run like they were in the 2000s.

Pop stars like Swift, Sabrina Carpenter and Olivia Rodrigo are among those who still lean on videos heavily to build out the visual world for each of their albums' eras.

Swift, who broke the record for most MTV VMA wins ever last weekend, is known for big budget productions which fans trawl through for Easter eggs - clues that could point to something else she has planned.

She also often enlists the help of her star-studded contact book, with her recent video for Opalite jam-packed with famous faces , including Graham Norton, Lewis Capaldi, Cillian Murphy, Domhnall Gleeson and Jodie Turner-Smith.

However, the music video was released exclusively on Spotify and Apple Music in February, and did not appear on YouTube until 48 hours later.

Industry analysts speculated at the time that the exclusivity period was due to a change in the US chart rules, where songs streamed on YouTube will no longer count towards the Top 100.

This change came into place in January, with YouTube saying it was ending its decade-long partnership with Billboard as it claimed the chart uses an "outdated formula that weights subscription-supported streams higher than ad-supported".

"This doesn't reflect how fans engage with music today and ignores the massive engagement from fans who don't have a subscription," it added.

And while most artists don't have Swift-level budgets to start with, this change may have further discouraged US artists' to throw a lot of money into creating elaborate music videos.

However, in international markets like the world of K-Pop, creating visually aesthetic music videos featuring polished choreography has become essential when promoting the act to a global audience.

The genre's superstars like BTS and Blackpink often also release dance practice videos and behind-the-scenes clips alongside traditional music videos.

These variations offer them more content to clip up for social media, and also helps drive up their streaming numbers and global chart positions.

Cofie feels the rise of platforms like TikTok, Instagram and YouTube has "100%" changed the way videos are consumed and therefore, how they are created.

But she doesn't see this as a "blow" to the industry and isn't "discouraged that things are changing so quickly".

"It kind of pushes us to think: 'Okay, how can each scene, each still be the one that captures people's attention?'," she says.

"We don't have five minutes anymore. We've actually got two minutes, sometimes less.

"I think it pushes us as creatives to think how can we get the point across quickly in the best way possible."

Gener8ion and Swedish rapper Yung Lean's cinematic music video for their collaboration track Storm is a testament to how a short mesmerising visual moment can make a song go viral online.

The scene from within the full video sees Lean, acting as a teenage bully, stand amongst a group of dancers who are also dressed in school uniforms as they perform hypnotic, synchronised choreography .

They recreated the routine at the VMAs, and while it lost out on the coveted video of the year award to Swift's The Fate of Ophelia, clips of the performance once again have flooded social media.

Cofie admits it has been "really tough" to come up with "new creative ideas" like this since short clips have boomed post-pandemic, but says she is continually inspired by new music videos.

And her advice to artists and crews who still want to create music videos?

"It's cliche, but just to continue being creative and just exploring every corner of your mind, any idea that you have, just do it," she says.

"Don't worry that it's already been done and it's not original because each and every person's interpretation or perspective is different."
