articles.title: The Backstory: 10 years of surgical strikes, the 10 days after Uri
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Ten years ago, on the night of September 28-29, 2016, Indian Army commandos crossed the Line of Control and carried out surgical strikes on
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Ten years ago, on the night of September 28-29, 2016, Indian Army commandos crossed the Line of Control and carried out surgical strikes on terrorist launch pads in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.The operation, carried out in response to the Pakistan-sponsored Uri terror attack, marked a hard-hitting response to Pakistan for sheltering and cultivating terror on its soil.It was the first time India responded not with a traditional full-fledged war, but with a calibrated and deliberate military operation against Islamabad-backed terror infrastructure across the border.It was also a demonstration of the more assertive counter-terrorism approach that the Modi government would later associate with its “New India” and “zero tolerance” messaging.But the story of the surgical strikes did not begin on the night of September 28.It began 10 days earlier, in a burning Army camp in Uri.ALSO READ: 18: When Uri came under attackAt around 5.30am on September 18, four heavily armed terrorists attacked the Army's 12th Brigade headquarters in Jammu and Kashmir's Uri, close to the Line of Control.The attack was on a rear administrative camp next to the brigade headquarters.The timing was particularly devastating. Troops were in the middle of a changeover, with an advance party of the incoming 6 Bihar unit in the process of replacing the outgoing 10 Dogra unit.Many soldiers were housed in temporary tents. Explosions and gunfire triggered a fire that spread through the camp.Seventeen soldiers were killed in the initial attack. Two others later succumbed to their injuries, taking the toll to 19.The four attackers were killed then and there.For the families, however, the numbers told only part of the story.In Rajasthan, Havaldar Nimb Singh Rawat's family was preparing to receive his body on what would have been his 48th birthday. A member of 6 Bihar, Rawat had routinely spent his birthdays on duty because his family lived away in Rajsamand district. He left behind his wife, four daughters and a young son.In Samba, 10-year-old Vansh, the son of Havildar Ravi Paul Salotra of 10 Dogra, said he wanted to fulfil his father's dream of becoming an Army doctor.The attack had suddenly turned a distant security crisis into funerals, grieving families and children asking questions.The first response: 'Will not go unpunished'Prime Minister Narendra Modi's first response came within hours.“We strongly condemn the cowardly terror attack in Uri. I assure the nation that those behind this despicable attack will not go unpunished,” PM Modi said.He also said the country saluted those martyred and that their service would always be remembered.The government began examining the attack, including the identity and possible origins of the attackers.Then-home minister Rajnath Singh cancelled a planned visit to Russia and the US and convened a security review in Delhi.“Pakistan is a terrorist state and it should be identified and isolated as such,” Rajnath Singh said on September 18, adding that there were indications that the attackers were highly trained, heavily armed and specially equipped.However, the public anger and government's rhetoric did not immediately translate into military strike.September 19: The question of retaliationWithin 24 hours, the government had begun examining possible responses.National security adviser Ajit Doval chaired a meeting of senior intelligence and military officials, according to contemporary reports, with options being prepared for the Prime Minister.One line attributed to the discussions captured the government's thinking: India would avenge the deaths, but “at a time of our choosing”.Outside the government, the demand for retaliation was growing.BJP general secretary Ram Madhav wrote on Facebook: “For one tooth, the complete jaw.”The expression reflected the anger after Uri. But inside the security establishment, the calculations were more complicated.Pakistan had heightened its alert along the LoC and an immediate strike risked escalation.This was the first crucial decision of the 10-day story.India would respond.But it would decide when, where and how.September 20-22: From anger to optionsThe government began weighing its choices.Diplomatic pressure was one part of the response. Within hours of the Uri attack, Indian missions abroad were asked to mobilise international condemnation of the attack.Then-external affairs mnister Sushma Swaraj would subsequently use the UN platform to attack Pakistan's support for terrorism.But the military option was also being examined.The Army was already monitoring terrorist infrastructure across the LoC. The DGMO would later say that almost 20 infiltration attempts had been foiled by the Army at or close to the LoC during 2016. India had also recovered GPS devices and other material that it said pointed to Pakistan as the source of the infiltration network.The question was no longer simply whether India could strike.It was whether it could strike in a way that was precise, limited and militarily useful.September 23: The plan takes shapeBy the third week of September, the military option was becoming more concrete.The targets were terrorist launch pads close to the LoC, where India believed militants were preparing to infiltrate Jammu and Kashmir.The proposed operation was not conceived as a conventional attack on Pakistan.The intended targets were terrorist infrastructure. The troops would cross the LoC, strike the launch pads and withdraw.The political leadership had to weigh the possibility that Pakistan would retaliate. The military had to work out routes, timings, surveillance and extraction.It was a narrow window between sending a message and triggering something much bigger. There was also a risk of indulging in a war with nuclear-armed neighbour.September 24: PM Modi's warningOn September 24, PM Narendra Modi met the chiefs of the Army and Air Force and the vice chief of the Navy, with NSA Ajit Doval also present, as discussions focused on the security situation and India’s response to the Uri attack.Later that day, speaking at a BJP rally in Kerala's Kozhikode, he addressed the families of the soldiers killed in Uri.India will never forget the sacrifices of our soldiers.PM warned that those responsible would be held accountable.The signal was becoming unmistakable. But the military operation remained secret.That evening, there was still no public indication that Indian Special Forces were preparing to cross the LoC.September 25-27: Preparing the menThe next few days were quieter in public, but crucial behind the scenes.According to Manohar Parrikar Institute under defence ministry, the Special Forces contingent selected for the operation was divided into smaller groups and moved towards the LoC, close to the Army’s forward positions. Later accounts of the operation said the teams moved after last light, crossed gaps in their own minefields and began closing in on the identified targets.The terrain itself was a challenge. The minefields ahead of Indian defences remained a constant danger, with mines sometimes shifting because of heavy rains and landslides. As the teams moved closer, the target areas were kept under watch for any changes that could affect the mission.At the designated hour, the teams struck.They then began their withdrawal, moving back towards their positions before daybreak.For the soldiers preparing to cross the LoC, this was no longer about speeches in Delhi.It was about moving through difficult terrain in darkness, reaching the targets, completing the mission and making it back safely.The Army would later say the operation was based on “very credible and specific information” about terrorist teams positioned at launch pads along the LoC and preparing to infiltrate and carry out attacks.The political leadership, meanwhile, kept the circle of people aware of the operation tightly controlled.September 28: The night India crossed the LoCAs darkness fell on September 28, the operation entered its final phase.Special Forces teams moved towards their designated targets.In the early hours of September 29, they crossed the Line of Control and entered the areas under Pakistan's illegal occupation where the Army had identified terrorist launch pads.The Army later said the teams struck several launch pads across multiple sectors along the LoC. After completing their mission, they began withdrawing before dawn.The operation was over.Then came the second, equally important decision. India would tell the world what it had done.September 29: 'Surgical strikes'The announcement came that morning.Then-DGMO Lt Gen Ranbir Singh appeared before the media and said the Army had conducted “surgical strikes” at several launch pads.The decision, he said, followed “very credible and specific information” that terrorist teams had positioned themselves at launch pads along the LoC with the aim of infiltrating Jammu and Kashmir and carrying out terrorist strikes in India.The Army said the strikes had caused “significant casualties” to terrorists and those supporting them.Singh also made clear that the operation had ended, saying there were no plans for further continuation of the strikes.India was not merely signalling that it had retaliated. It was publicly acknowledging that its forces had crossed the LoC and struck what it described as terrorist launch pads.Pakistan rejected India's account of a surgical strike and said its soldiers had come under fire.For the Union government, however, the operation had acquired a significance beyond the battlefield.It had chosen to publicly own the operation and put its account of the events on record.What made 2016 differentCross-LoC raids were not unprecedented.Indian troops had conducted tactical operations across the LoC before. What changed in 2016 was the combination of political authorisation, the scale of the operation and, above all, the decision to publicly acknowledge it.The government did not leave the operation as an unconfirmed military action.The then-DGMO briefed the country.The term “surgical strikes” entered India's national-security vocabulary.And the PM Modi-led government presented the operation as a calibrated response to terrorism, rather than the opening move in a conventional war.That distinction was crucial.India had chosen to hit terrorist infrastructure without declaring war on Pakistan.From Uri to BalakotHowever, the September 2016 strikes did not end Pakistan-manufactured terrorism.In February 2019, a Jaish-e-Mohammed suicide bomber attacked a CRPF convoy in Pulwama, killing 40 personnel.Twelve days later, on February 26, the Indian Air Force carried out an air strike on a Jaish-e-Mohammed facility at Balakot in mainland Pakistan.The response had now moved beyond the LoC as Balakot is close to international border and situated in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.India had demonstrated that air power, too, could be used against terrorist infrastructure across the border.The 2016 template had evolved.Then came Operation SindoorIn 2025, the response was broader still.Following the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack, which killed 26 people, India launched Operation Sindoor on May 7.The government said the armed forces struck nine terrorist infrastructure sites in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir. It described the initial strikes as "focused and measured".The strikes were not limited to terrorist infrastructure. After Pakistan launched waves of drones and missiles towards Indian territory, New Delhi expanded its response to include military targets.India then struck Pakistani military installations, targeting 11 airbases as part of the broader operation.The confrontation subsequently expanded, involving missiles, drones, air-defence systems and attacks on military targets before the Pakistani side pleaded India for a ceasefire on land, air and water.On Pakistan DGMO's request, India announced ceasefire on May 10.The technology and scale were vastly different from 2016.But the sequence was familiar.A decade later: What changed?The Army's counterterrorism architecture has now evolved.The response now relies heavily on intelligence-led operations, surveillance, drones, satellite imagery, counter-infiltration measures and precision weapons.A decade later, the battlefield is increasingly shaped by sensors, drones, precision weapons and real-time intelligence.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: School tied to history's greatest ruler reveals clues about his life before he rose to power
articles.summary: Archaeologists at Mieza in ancient Macedonia uncovered lecture rooms and mosaic floors within Royal Gymnasium complex long tied to Aristotle and Alexander the Great.
articles.body: New discoveries at an ancient site in Greece are revealing the remains of a sprawling royal complex where young Macedonians studied and trained — offering new clues about a school tied to one of history's most legendary rulers. The recent finds were announced by the Hellenic Ministry of Culture, part of the Greek government, in early September. The excavation centers on Mieza, an ancient Macedonian city in northern Greece, where archaeologists have been uncovering a sprawling complex known as the Royal Gymnasium. ANCIENT PALACE DISCOVERY CHALLENGES THE MYTH BEHIND SPARTA'S RISE TO POWER It has long been believed, based on ancient accounts, that a young Alexander the Great was taught by Aristotle at Mieza. The site dates to the reign of Philip II, Alexander the Great's father, in the fourth century B.C. Archaeologists began excavating the site in 2024, gradually uncovering evidence of an expansive complex where young Macedonians studied, trained and dined. This year's excavation has focused on the eastern side of the complex, including the palaestra and the "Didaskaleion," or teaching area, where archaeologists identified lecture rooms with stone benches. 'DIG OF THE CENTURY' BENEATH NOTRE DAME REVEALS MYSTERIOUS MARKINGS, ANCIENT SECRETS One of the most significant discoveries was a three-part complex spanning more than 1,700 square feet within the Didaskaleion, or teaching area, according to the Hellenic Ministry of Culture. The space includes a central entry room and two banquet rooms with surviving mosaic floors and raised platforms that once held dining couches. Though the buildings were destroyed by the Romans after the second Battle of Pydna in 148 B.C., officials noted that "significant architectural remains have survived." Those remains are now giving researchers a clearer picture of what education may have looked like for young Macedonian elites. DAMAGED FRAGMENT DEEMED 'UNREMARKABLE' TURNS OUT TO BE RARE PIECE OF HOMER'S 'ODYSSEY' HISTORY Alexandra F. Morris, a lecturer in ancient history at Queen's University Belfast, told Fox News Digital that ancient texts link Alexander and Aristotle to Mieza, while the archaeological discoveries are providing a physical setting for those accounts. "What we have in the ancient text is writers like Plutarch, basically just a line in the text saying that Alexander was taught by Aristotle at Mieza," Morris told Fox News Digital. "The case seems to be getting stronger." "But now we have an actual building to put that story to, which is really exciting." The evidence makes the identification increasingly compelling, the historian said, though she cautioned that researchers cannot yet definitively say Aristotle taught Alexander in this particular complex. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "There is no inscription that directly names the site," said Morris. "I think the identification we have right now is a strong argument, but it’s still only an argument that Aristotle potentially taught Alexander here." "But the case seems to be getting stronger." Education at an ancient gymnasium looked far different from a typical school day today, Morris also noted. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "You would go there to train physically as part of your day," Morris said. "So you would compete in sports games like pankration, which was a form of wrestling. You would then go and listen to lectures." "You were there to learn, but you were also there to learn how to build loyalty with other elite men who were there," the historian added. articles.title: Journalist ascends to throne in Uganda kingdom after succession dispute
articles.summary: Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma succeeds King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who died last month.
articles.body:
A journalist has been crowned king of Uganda’s Tooro Kingdom, becoming the 13th monarch of the Batooro people in a ceremony marking the ⁠end of a succession dispute .

Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma succeeded King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, whose death last month from cancer at age 34 triggered a feud after his mother said a previously undisclosed son was entitled to the throne.

Uganda is a ⁠constitutional republic governed by an elected president, but four pre-colonial kingdoms remain influential symbols of identity and heritage despite not having political power.

A 21-member committee from the royal Babiito clan selected Kijanangoma, 56, who is Oyo Nyimba’s cousin.

Kijanangoma took the royal ‌name Edward Rukidi Nyabongo I in a traditional ceremony that included the slaughter of a bull and sprinkling of a hen’s blood in Tooro’s capital, Fort Portal.

Nyabongo I walked to Karuziika Palace from midnight to 3am on Tuesday (21:00 GMT on Monday to 00:00 GMT on Tuesday) before taking part in a mock battle for the crown.

Former colleagues of Nyabongo ⁠I at the state broadcaster UBC, where he worked as a news anchor and editor, described him as humble and down to earth.

The selection of Nyabongo I as king was widely contested because he wasn’t in the direct line of succession, and the coronation took place despite objections from Oyo Nyimba’s mother, Best Kemigisa, and sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale.

They say the late king left behind a young son and a will ‌naming him as his heir. The claim to the throne has led to increasing disquiet within the community on the selection of Nyabongo I.

The reason for Kemigisa’s withholding of the identity of the heir remains unclear.

Critics said, however, that Oyo’s alleged child would have to have been introduced to the kingdom’s elders when his father was still alive to become a legitimate heir, if he even exists at all.

articles.title: Psychology says children who copy their parents are building their identity through everyday habits and emotions they observe at home
articles.summary: A child pretending to speak on the phone exactly like a parent, copying the way they sit or repeating a phrase they hear every day may look like simple
articles.body: A child pretending to speak on the phone exactly like a parent, copying the way they sit or repeating a phrase they hear every day may look like simple imitation. But these small moments can reveal an important part of how children learn. Psychology has long recognised that children learn by observing people around them, particularly the adults who care for them. Parents are among the people children encounter most frequently, which means everyday behaviour at home can become an important source of information about how to communicate, respond to situations and interact with others. This does not mean children simply become exact copies of their parents. Their development is shaped by many influences, including temperament, relationships, peers, school and the wider environment. But what they repeatedly see at home can become part of the behavioural patterns they learn and practise.Psychology says children learn by watching before they understand everythingOne of the best-known explanations for imitation comes from psychologist Albert Bandura's work on observational learning. His research helped establish the idea that people can learn behaviours by watching others rather than experiencing every behaviour themselves. For children, parents and caregivers can therefore become important behavioural models. A child may watch a parent cook and later pretend to cook during play. They may see a parent exercising and imitate the movements. They may observe how adults greet guests, speak to service workers, respond to mistakes or deal with frustration. The same process can apply to less obvious behaviours.Children may notice whether adults say thank you, apologise after making a mistake, listen when someone is speaking or become impatient when things go wrong. Over time, repeated observations can provide children with examples of how people behave in everyday situations. This is one reason the ordinary moments of family life can matter. Children do not need a formal lesson for every behaviour they learn. The Harvard Center on the Developing Child also emphasises the importance of responsive relationships between children and caring adults. Its research-based resources describe "serve and return" interactions, in which adults respond to children's sounds, gestures, expressions and interests. These back-and-forth interactions help support early social, emotional and language development.Children can also learn how to handle emotions by watching parentsImitation is not limited to physical actions. Children also observe emotional responses. A child who repeatedly sees an adult calmly deal with a stressful situation may learn that frustration can be managed without immediately reacting. Similarly, seeing adults acknowledge their mistakes and apologise can provide an example of accountability. This does not mean parents need to hide every difficult emotion. In fact, children can learn useful lessons when they see adults experience frustration, sadness or uncertainty and then handle those feelings appropriately.The important factor is the overall pattern. A parent who loses patience and later says sorry is demonstrating that mistakes can be acknowledged and repaired. A parent who asks for help can show that needing support is normal. A parent who listens carefully can demonstrate how respectful communication works. The Harvard Center on the Developing Child notes that responsive relationships help provide a foundation for healthy development and can also help buffer children against the effects of stress. This does not mean every parental behaviour will automatically be copied. Children interpret what they observe, and different children can respond differently to the same environment. Still, repeated experiences can become meaningful parts of their learning environment.Parents do not need to be perfect role modelsThe idea that children are always watching can sometimes make parents feel that they must behave perfectly. Psychology does not support such an unrealistic expectation. Parents will make mistakes, become frustrated and occasionally respond in ways they later regret. What can be valuable for children is seeing what happens afterwards. When a parent apologises, explains what went wrong and tries again, the child receives another lesson: mistakes do not have to be hidden, and relationships can be repaired. The Harvard Center on the Developing Child describes early experiences and relationships as important influences on developing brain architecture and later learning, behaviour and health. It also stresses that development is shaped by a broad range of experiences, not by one isolated interaction.So when a child copies a parent's expressions, routines or reactions, it may be more than an amusing family moment. The child is experimenting with behaviours and learning what different actions mean. Parents are not their children's only teachers, and children eventually develop their own personalities, beliefs and choices. But the patterns children repeatedly encounter at home can give them an early framework for understanding relationships, emotions and everyday life. That is why the smallest habits can sometimes carry the biggest lessons. A child may appear to be simply copying a parent, but behind that imitation is a developing person trying to understand the world and find their own place in it.You use AI every day. articles.title: French hard-right leader Bardella accuses opponents of 'total war' after claims of antisemitism
articles.summary: National Rally President Jordan Bardella says he will sue for libel over comments he is accused of making as a young activist.
articles.body:
The president of France's hard-right National Rally (RN), Jordan Bardella, has said he will sue for libel after a report published antisemitic comments that it alleged he had made as a young activist.

The Mediapart website released what it said was the result of "several months" of investigation into "dozens of written conversations" Bardella allegedly had in 2013.

With seven months to go before France's presidential elections, Bardella condemned "the beginnings of a total war" aimed at destabilising his party, and RN presidential candidate Marine Le Pen said she had total confidence in him.

The alleged remarks included blatantly antisemitic tropes, and Bardella said they were an attempt to destroy his political career.

Mediapart did not produce screen-grabs of any of the alleged remarks. It said it had "independently authenticated" the conversations, which came from "a bigger documentary base corroborated by witness statements".

But Bardella, 31 – who is a likely prime minister if Le Pen wins the presidential election – said the allegations were a fabrication aimed at derailing the RN's increasingly confident bid for power.

"Everything is going to be done to destabilise the campaign," he told CNews television on Monday night. "Either Mediapart is running this operation itself, or it is being manipulated by interested parties.

"Of course I have instructed my lawyer to sue for libel."

Le Pen said the alleged remarks "seem so weird that they can only be a forgery – one of those dirty tricks for which Mediapart appears to hold the secret".

Among the statements that Mediapart alleges Bardella made when he was 17 or 18 are: "All the banks are owned by Jews"; "The Jew has to dominate other people, crush them and rob them"; and "What they want is a new world order dominated by Israel, with of course Jerusalem as its capital."

Mediapart is an avowedly leftwing website which has exposed a number of scandals over the years, though its targets have been politicians of all stripes.

The French hard right is riding higher than ever in pre-election polls, with the latest this week, from Toluna-Harris, showing Le Pen a clear victor over whatever rival she faces in the crucial second round in May.

According to the survey, Le Pen would pick up 35-36% of the vote in the multi-candidate first round. Her likely opponent in the two-way run-off would be Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the radical left who she would eradicate with 69% of the vote.

But in a stark warning for the political establishment, the poll showed that she would also easily beat the most popular centrist candidate Edouard Philippe, with a score of 57%.

On Sunday the RN received another boost when results of a partial election for the upper house of parliament, the Senate, produced for the first time enough seats for the party to form an official group.

Under Marine Le Pen, daughter of the historic party founder Jean-Marie Le Pen, the RN has made huge efforts to distance itself from the French far-right's antisemitic roots.

Last year Bardella was the first senior figure from the party to be invited to Israel, for a conference on antisemitism.

Today the party regards militant Islam as a pre-eminent threat – a position it shares with many Jews. The RN even styles itself as a "shield for the Jewish community".

The alleged comments from Bardella throw back to a current of far-right thinking that Mediapart says has never been eradicated but only covered up in the new-look party.

Leftwing politicians called on Bardella to resign, and the head of the Jewish umbrella organisation Crif, Yonathan Arfi, said the alleged comments "were an illustration of the limits of the RN's clean-up act".

But RN deputy Jean-Philippe Tanguy said the source of the allegations was disaffected members of the party who had been expelled years ago because of their antisemitic ideas.

"From what I know, it is the antisemitic rabble that were so bravely purged by Marine Le Pen. At the start of the 2010s, they were numerous and well-organised, but they were defeated. These people have always had it in for us."

articles.title: 'I was lured into a trap': Evan Gershkovich on moment that led to 16 months in Russian jail
articles.summary: The US journalist says he realised he was a "a pawn in a greater game" when he was not interrogated or tortured by FSB agents.
articles.body:
US journalist Evan Gershkovich has said that he knew he was being set up by Russia when he was arrested by FSB agents and accused of being a spy.

In an interview with Radio 4's Today programme, Gershkovich spoke about the moment he realised he had been "lured into a trap" when masked men surrounded him at a restaurant in 2023, and detained him.

"I'm not interrogated, I'm not tortured… I'm accused of espionage," he said, describing a sense of relief: "They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage - a pawn in a greater game".

Gershkovich, now 34, was sentenced to 16 years in prison, but freed 16 months later as part of a high-profile prisoner swap deal .

Gershkovich had been living in Russia since 2017, and was the Wall Street Journal's foreign correspondent in Moscow when he was arrested - he is now based in Berlin, Germany. He and his employer have always maintained that the charges were false.

On the day he was arrested, Gershkovich was in Yekaterinburg - about 1,600km (1,000 miles) east of Moscow - meeting someone who he thought was a source for a story.

They were sitting in a half-empty dining hall "and a group of about half-dozen masked men marched in and said 'I think we booked that table'." An odd phrase, Gershkovich said, but on reflection it is clever because it "freezes you in place".

The two men stood up and Gershkovich was told he was under arrest by the notorious and powerful FSB, Russia's domestic security service.

"It's at that moment that you realise it's something really serious… When it's the FSB, you know it's been planned."

What about the man he'd been meeting? Gershkovich saw him disappear into the crowd.

Not long after his arrest, the journalist said he realised that the fact he was not being interrogated or tortured - common tactics used by Russia's security service on spies - likely meant that he was being treated more like a commodity, not a true enemy of the state.

"I have this odd moment - a sense of relief flooding over me," he said. "I realised they're not treating me like a real spy. They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage, a pawn in a greater game. That means it will take a while, but I won't be here for 12-20 years."

That realisation helped him stay "stable and disciplined in prison", but also gave him a unique way of predicting what might happen next - and one guess was a prisoner swap.

"I assumed that it would be really loud, that it would cause a global uproar. I mean, it's a foreign correspondent for the Wall Street Journal," he said - and he was right.

Media organisations around the world reported on the case, his face was on a billboard in Times Square and then-US President Joe Biden said he had "no higher priority" than bringing Gershkovich home.

The journalist believed that this was all part of Moscow's plan - to have a high-profile prisoner that it could swap for one of its own - and that was Vadim Krasikov , an assassin who was serving a life sentence in Germany.

"They [Moscow] got away with it in the sense that there were no sanctions imposed. And so they played it really smart, if you think about it cynically."

Gershkovich was held in Moscow's infamous Lefortovo jail, which has held some of the country's most high-profile inmates over the years, including political prisoners and dissidents. During the Great Terror of Joseph Stalin in the 1930s, torture and execution were commonplace.

He described it as a "really isolating experience", in a tiny space.

"That wears on you psychologically," Gershkovich said, but added that he was treated ok: "I was allowed to sleep, the food was fine."

Pictures of Gershkovich smiling at cameras during his court appearances in Moscow were broadcast around the world - and that was deliberate, he said - a way of showing that he was alright.

"I wanted to show people this kind of defiance... We know that this is a fabricated case, and so if this is a game of theatre, let's not let [Moscow] have it play out the way they want it to."

But he stressed that not everyone's time in a Russian prison is like his: "Some people... get tortured. They get broken as human beings, deprived of food, of hot water for showers, told that they're never going to see their families again. I was treated completely differently."

Gershkovich compared his experience to the case of Ukrainian journalist Viktoriia Roshchyna , who died while in Russian captivity in 2024, aged 27. Months later, when her body was finally returned, it reportedly showed signs of torture and her organs had been removed.

Gershkovich knew there was a prisoner swap planned three weeks before it happened - an "excruciating" time, he said, "because now every day is painfully long".

When it finally did happen, on 1 August 2024, it was a moment of "pure joy". But then "the joy fades, the adrenaline subsides, and you're faced with the reality of having to return to normal life again."

Gershkovich said this period was difficult and sometimes overwhelming. He wasn't sleeping, suffered panic attacks in large crowds and had a short temper because he was trying to hold in his emotions.

He has seen therapists who specialise in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and said writing a book on his ordeal also helped.

And what about a return to Russia? Gershkovich has a deep history with the country - his parents moved to the US from the Soviet Union in the 1970s. He grew up in a Russian-speaking home, with a Russian name, moved there when he was 25 and made many friends, including his Russian girlfriend.

"I would hope to get back one day, but I guess we'll have to see what comes after [Russian President Vladimir] Putin. And it's not completely clear that the next government will be any better."

articles.title: Singapore crocodile: Man charged over AI image
articles.summary: The defendant could face jail or a fine after the image sparked a search operation in the city’s largest reservoir.
articles.body:
Police in Singapore have charged a man who is accused of posting an AI-generated image of a saltwater crocodile in a popular reservoir.

Ye Lin was charged with communicating a false message and obstructing the course of justice for allegedly deleting the picture and the application he used.

The fake image caused public concern, authorities allege. The national water agency suspended its work at the city-state's largest reservoir for two days last month after receiving information that a crocodile had been spotted.

Ye Lin, who is from Myanmar, told the court through an interpreter that he intended to plead guilty, according to local media reports.

The national water agency said it was alerted to a crocodile sighting in Pandan Reservoir on 20 August. Agency officials and national parks staff conducted search and capture operations in the area. The Singapore Rowing Association and Singapore Canoe Federation were told the suspend their activities.

But the following day, the water agency confirmed that the crocodile image was fake and reported it to the police.

The case will return to court in November and Ye Lin could face a prison sentence and a large fine if he is found guilty.

In Singapore, sending a false message is punishable by up to three years in prison, a fine of up to S$10,000 (about US$7,800; £5,900), or both. Obstructing justice carries up to seven years in prison, a fine, or both.

Police allege that Ye Lin created the photo of the crocodile using artificial intelligence before sending it to a colleague.

"The man subsequently deleted the image and the related application in an attempt to conceal his actions," the police statement said.

It is not clear how the national water agency was notified of the false photo that Ye Lin sent to his colleague.

articles.title: In 2023, Texas mogul Felix Sorkin paid $36 million for an 11,000-sq-ft Coral Gables home designed by Alfred Browning Parker; months later, the 1963 modernist house was demolished for a replacement
articles.summary: A multimillionaire property developer from Texas has demolished a historic waterfront mansion in Coral Gables, Florida, only months after buying the
articles.body: A multimillionaire property developer from Texas has demolished a historic waterfront mansion in Coral Gables, Florida, only months after buying the estate for $36 million. The demolition has sparked anger among local preservationists and architectural historians. Felix Sorkin, founder of the Houston-based manufacturing company General Technologies, bought the 11,000-square-foot property in mid-2023. Known as the Wood Residence, the estate was designed in 1963 by Alfred Browning Parker, one of South Florida’s best-known modernist architects. Despite efforts by local heritage advocates to save the landmark, bulldozers tore down the residence to make way for a large modern mansion, the Miami Herald reported. The loss of the home shows the growing conflict in South Florida between rising land prices and efforts to protect mid-century architectural history.Architectural legacy reduced to rubbleBuilt on a prime 1.2-acre lot along Biscayne Bay, the Wood Residence was widely seen as a fine example of organic architecture. Parker, a protégé of Frank Lloyd Wright, designed the home with natural materials, including heart-pine woodwork, native stone walls and large glass panels. These features helped connect the indoor spaces with the surrounding tropical landscape. According to research cited by the Miami Herald, Parker designed the house to make the most of natural ventilation and light. These features were central to his modernist style, which was designed for the local climate. The house also had a striking sloped roof, custom mahogany cabinets and an open floor plan that influenced mid-century home design across the region. Preservationists said the home was one of the finest surviving examples of Parker’s residential work. However, the property did not have formal local historic designation. Because of this, Sorkin was legally allowed to apply for a standard demolition permit after completing the purchase.Local regulations fail to prevent lossThe quick demolition shocked community members and local architecture groups. Coral Gables has long been known for strict zoning rules and historic preservation codes. Properties must go through a specific review process to receive protected status. The Miami Herald reported that the Coral Gables Historic Preservation Board had not designated the Wood Residence as a landmark before the sale. Under local ordinance, if a property owner does not seek historic designation, or if city officials do not begin an emergency preservation review before permit applications are processed, private property rights usually take priority. Local preservation advocates said they were frustrated by regulatory gaps that allow important historic buildings to be demolished without a public hearing. Members of the Docomomo US Florida chapter, an organisation focused on protecting modern architecture, said mid-century homes along valuable waterfront areas remain especially vulnerable to rising land prices.Rising land values drive redevelopment trendThe demolition reflects a wider economic trend in South Florida’s luxury real estate market. In areas such as Coral Gables, Miami Beach and Key Biscayne, the land itself can be worth more than the historic buildings on it. Property records sourced by the Miami Herald show that wealthy buyers are increasingly buying older estates mainly for the size and location of the land. Buyers often choose to demolish existing buildings and construct larger, ultra-modern compounds. These new homes can offer higher ceilings, stronger hurricane protection and larger amenities that older designs may not easily support. Sorkin’s $36 million purchase set a significant price benchmark for the neighborhood. Construction plans filed with the city show that the Texas industrialist plans to build a new custom luxury residence on the cleared Biscayne Bay property.Legacy of Alfred Browning ParkerAlfred Browning Parker, who died in 2011, created more than 6,000 residential and commercial designs during a career that lasted six decades. His work received national attention and appeared in major architecture publications during the 1950s and 1960s. This included House Beautiful, which devoted entire issues to his climate-conscious home designs. Architectural historians consider Parker an important figure in adapting modernism to subtropical areas. He used local materials, deep roof edges for shade and direct connections to natural waterways. These choices helped set an example for sustainable coastal design long before the idea became widely used in architecture. With the Wood Residence now gone, preservation groups are urging municipal leaders in Miami-Dade County to update historical surveys and identify vulnerable mid-century buildings before similar sales take place. City officials have acknowledged the community’s concerns, but no immediate changes to the Coral Gables historic preservation ordinance have been enacted.You use AI every day. articles.title: Lindsay Clancy defense returns to court to argue there’s no evidence she killed her children
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy and her legal team returned to court on Tuesday, arguing that the state of Massachusetts failed to prove she killed her children — a claim that prosecutors called “laughable.”
articles.body: Lindsay Clancy and her legal team returned to court on Tuesday, arguing that the state of Massachusetts failed to prove she killed her children — a claim that prosecutors called “laughable.” This marks the first hearing since Clancy’s triple murder trial ended in a mistrial earlier this month. The hearing in Plymouth Superior Court, which began just before 10 a.m., included a number of motions filed since the trial concluded. Judge William Sullivan immediately punted some of those motions to a later date, noting that he, and some parties, were not ready for them to be argued. One of those motions is defense attorney Kevin Reddington’s effort to dismiss Clancy’s case. Sullivan heard arguments as a part of that motion Tuesday, but pushed his decision on those arguments, as well as those relating to other motions, until Nov. 2. The judge also declined to set a new trial date, with both Reddington and prosecutors agreeing that with so much still to decide, it could be premature to do so. Reddington on Tuesday offered arguments on Massachusetts’ Rule 25, which states that if prosecutors do not argue their case effectively, the defendant should be found not guilty. He first lamented that Clancy had been demonized by politicians “from Donald Trump all the way down.” And in a new approach that seemed contrary to the defense’s strategy in the trial, Reddington then argued that there is no proof Clancy killed her children, and that the commonwealth did not provide evidence she did so. Prosecutors, in response, called that allegation “laughable.” “And now, for the first time, the defendant is arguing that there’s no evidence that she did this,” Assistant District Attorney Shanan Buckingham said. “I’d suggest to you that the entire record is voluminous as to the information supporting the fact that she did this.” Sullivan said he would take that motion “under advisement.” Clancy, 36, is accused of fatally strangling her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — using exercise bands Jan. 24, 2023. Her defense team, led by Reddington, argued she was in a state of psychosis at the time of the killings, a result of the postpartum psychosis she was suffering from, and was therefore unaware of and unable to control her actions. The prosecution, however, said that Clancy knowingly planned the killings ahead of time, arguing for a first-degree murder conviction. After a weekslong trial, the jury could not come to a unanimous decision. The group of nine women and three men deadlocked three times, forcing the judge to declare a mistrial Sept. 4. After the trial concluded, several jurors spoke publicly and described a single holdout juror who they said refused to meet the required reasonable-doubt standard. Eleven of the jurors wanted to find Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility, and the holdout wanted to convict, they have said. That man has since identified himself as Michael P. Desronvil. The jurors said he was the sole reason they could not reach a conclusion, describing someone who refused to participate in negotiations and seemed uninterested in hearing the other jurors out. Desronvil has denied the other jurors’ allegations, saying in a statement that he “didn’t have any doubts” Clancy was guilty. In a statement given to Fox News’ Sean Hannity on Monday, Desronvil said he wants to turn the focus away from him and back to Clancy’s children. “I know the whole focus has been on me, but we want to reel everything back and put the focus on the three angels that is that hand — the ones that can’t speak for themselves, the ones that can’t defend themselves, and the one that can’t fight the battles, and those are Cora, Dawson, and Callan,” Desronvil said in the statement. Also Monday, the commonwealth of Massachusetts filed a motion asking Reddington to stop making “extrajudicial statements to the media” ahead of a potential retrial. In the days after the first trial concluded, Reddington spoke with several media outlets, including NBC News, to outline what happened in court and what he’d like to see for his client going forward. The Boston Globe and the local CBS station WBZ-TV jointly filed an opposition to the motion, claiming that it would restrict free speech. Sullivan decided to hear the arguments related to both of these motions at the November trial date. Reddington got heated toward the end of the hearing, angrily stating he is “so tired” of people saying he has persecuted and attacked the holdout juror. In his motion, he argued that the judge should have dismissed the juror after the foreperson told Sullivan he was refusing to follow jury instructions.

articles.title: Estonia blames Russia for arson at defence company supplying Ukraine
articles.summary: Russia has been accused of launching sabotage attacks across a number of European Nato countries which have been helping Ukraine.
articles.body:
Russia was behind an arson attack on an Estonian defence company in the capital Tallinn last month, authorities say.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the attack on Milrem Robotics - which supplies Ukraine with unmanned military vehicles - was ordered by Russian special services, but gave no details.

Moscow has been accused of launching sabotage attacks in a number of Nato countries that have been helping Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbour in February 2022.

Russia denies such allegations and has been quick to reject the Estonian accusation, too. But EU countries have rushed to Estonia's support, adding such attacks will not deter them from helping Ukraine.

The attack on Milrem Robotics occurred on the night of 14-15 August.

Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said that, based on information collected by the country's Internal Security Service, "we can conclude with certainty that the arson attack... was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation".

Security service chief Margo Palloson told broadcaster ERR that Russia was "constantly planning, looking for opportunities, trying to find people who would carry out attacks", but that last month's arson attack was its first successful attack this year.

The foreign minister said the perpetrators had been arrested and Palloson said they were Latvians who had been living in Russia and taken part in previous attacks. Three suspects were arrested in Latvia and extradited to Estonia earlier this month.

Margus Tsahkna said that "this act of sabotage is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe, aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine".

French President Emmanuel Macron responded to Estonia's assessment, saying "the multiplication of these hostile acts represents a dangerous escalation by Russia, which will only lead it into a dead end".

He mentioned the incident at Leipzig airport in Germany in August, in which an explosive-laden drone was found near Ukrainian cargo planes.

"Russia needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine," Macron added.

An EU spokesman said the 27-member bloc would not cease supporting Ukraine.

Nato chief Mark Rutte urged European governments to stay calm and continue supporting Ukraine.

"Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies. It is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine. But Russia is failing. It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine," Rutte said.

Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect

Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack

Inside the Russian explosives plot that sent incendiary parcels to the UK

In August alone, Russia was either accused or suspected of the Leipzig airport attack in Germany, a major fire at a warehouse of a defence firm in Bulgaria, a large explosion at a munitions factory outside Rome in Italy, an attempted arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer in Slovakia, and two suspicious fires in Poland - the latest in a country which has reported several such attacks.

Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms that tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.

Estonia's internal security service, known as Kapo, said Russia was continuing to look for further opportunities for either sabotage or other hostile acts.

"Individuals recruited for such operations may be misled or manipulated and may be given false or fabricated justifications for their actions in an effort to conceal the involvement of the Russian state," Kapo head Palloson said .

Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.

On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman said "such statements are baseless, ill-considered, have absolutely no relation to reality, and lack any form of reasoning".

"We cannot and will not take such statements seriously," Dmitry Peskov said.

articles.title: Iran downplays possible role in Houthis’ recent Yemen victories
articles.summary: Iran has long been accused of links with the Houthis in Yemen, but how far do these links go?
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Strategic military victories in Yemen by the Tehran-allied Ansar Allah, also known as Houthis, have directed attention towards Iran’s role in the war against the internationally recognised Yemeni government.

According to recent US media reports, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) helped direct an offensive in western Yemen that solidified Houthi control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait and the port city of Mocha.

The Houthis gains on the coast coincide with Iran’s disruptions of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz to pressure Washington to lift its naval blockade, US media have reported in recent weeks.

IRGC advisers worked with front-line commanders, assisted with communications and satellite-intelligence analysis, and promised ongoing military support to the Houthis, according to unnamed officials and soldiers cited.

Iranian authorities have not commented on details of the latest allegations but have broadly denied directing the Houthis. They and the Houthis have long stressed the Yemeni group’s independence, despite their geopolitical views often converging.

The IRGC said it viewed the Houthis recent advances in Yemen as a “ divine triumph ” that followed years of steadfastness.

Earlier this week, President Masoud Pezeshkian rejected a connection between Iran and Houthi actions during an interview with Al Jazeera. He also urged Saudi Arabia, which supports the Yemeni government, and the Houthis to negotiate to end the war. But he did offer Iranian assistance in resolving their years-long conflict, which has included Houthi missile and drone attacks on cities in Saudi Arabia.

Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs earlier this month rejected a charge by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that the Houthis are a proxy of Iran. It also highlighted the dire humanitarian consequences of a Saudi blockade on Yemen.

In mid-July, an Iranian passenger aircraft attempted to break the blockade by landing in the Houthi-run airport in the capital Sanaa. The aircraft was redirected after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government bombed the airport shortly before it was due to land.

The aeroplane ended up touching down in Hodeidah, and a Houthi official denied government allegations that the plane carried IRGC personnel.

Iran’s authorities said the plane carried a Houthi delegation which had participated in the funeral of slain Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, as well as a number of Yemeni nationals who had received medical treatment in Iran.

This September, the Houthis captured Mocha, Dhubab and Mayyun (or Perim) Island , giving them command of Yemen’s west coast and the Bab al-Mandeb strait, which links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. It also cut the internationally recognised Yemeni government’s access to the Red Sea.

In September 2024, a confidential United Nations report leaked to US media claimed that, with the help of the IRGC, Lebanon’s Hezbollah and Iraqi specialists, the Houthis had grown “from a localised armed group with limited capabilities to a powerful military organisation”.

Members of the Houthis were receiving tactical and technical training outside Yemen and members were travelling on fake passports to Iran, Lebanon and Iraq, the report alleged.

Iran played an important advisory and logistical role, although it is important not to overstate it, Yemen expert and political risk researcher Nicholas Brumfield told Al Jazeera.

“Iran has had advisers embedded with the Houthis for years, the IRGC [and Hezbollah] is involved in senior Houthi decision-making, and Iran continues to supply weapons and technology to the Houthis,” Brumfield said.

“That said, the west coast offensive reportedly involved 76,000 Yemeni fighters that the Houthis raised using their own governance apparatuses, and there is increasing evidence of the Houthis possessing domestic military industrial capabilities.”

Intense fighting in Yemen has focused on strategic high ground around Taiz and Lahij, including the Kahboub Mountains, as the Houthis seek to consolidate their recent gains and government forces attempt to recoup losses.

With Yemeni government forces now positioned in more favourable mountainous terrain with air support, the Houthis are not expected to repeat the same rapid advances they achieved in September.

This was achieved through their ability to deploy large numbers of fighters with strategic backing against relatively untested government-linked forces in Mocha.

They also exploited continued divisions among Yemeni government-aligned forces, including technically compromising their communications and command-and-control, and the unwillingness or unpreparedness of Saudi Arabia to provide air support during the coastal campaign.

Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan travelled to Washington for talks with Rubio on Tuesday, while UAE Vice President Mansour bin Zayed is scheduled to visit Riyadh after an invitation by Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman. The UAE withdrew from Yemen after Saudi-backed government forces launched an offensive against Southern Transitional Council (STC) separatists, long accused of being supported by Abu Dhabi.

It is unknown why these meetings are taking place, but they come after conflicting reports about the level of support Washington is providing Saudi Arabia regarding Yemen. The US also reportedly declined Saudi requests for strikes in Yemen to support the government .

Since taking over Yemen’s west coast, the Houthis have stressed that they have no plans to disrupt Red Sea trade, but will continue to target Saudi-linked vessels.

US President Donald Trump said his administration had established contact with the group and was assured they would not target international shipping, at a time when global markets are in flux over disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

But since Yemen’s war restarted, the Houthis have successfully targeted several Saudi tankers and are believed to be behind disruptions to the critical East-West oil pipeline , as well as targeting multiple Saudi cities.

Both the Houthis and Tehran denied Saudi allegations that the Yemeni group was responsible for the launch of a drone towards the holy Muslim city of Mecca.

Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif told the UN General Assembly that any threat to Muslim holy sites in Mecca and Medina would constitute a “red line that must never be crossed”.

Pakistan and Turkiye, which have a defence pact with Riyadh, have so far refrained from entering the conflict despite sustained Houthi attacks on their ally Saudi Arabia.

The developments in Yemen have come as experts say Iran and the US appear to be on a course for military escalation , even as they maintain contact via mediators such as Pakistan, Qatar, Oman and Turkiye to reach a deal on reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Yemen expert Brumfield said that despite attempts to distinguish the two parties, it is fair to describe the Houthis as a very close ally of Iran.

“There is a great deal of trust between them and Iran, they’ll go out of their way to help Tehran, and the strategic alignment between the two is such that they rarely have irreconcilable interests,” he said.

But the implications of acknowledging clear Houthi-Iran links would put Riyadh in a difficult position, as Saudi Arabia has suffered from Houthi attacks, as well strikes from Tehran-backed Iraqi militias.

“Earlier in the war, this vulnerability pushed the Saudis to be incredibly conciliatory to Iran even amid intense attacks, and it may be Riyadh simply has no option but to capitulate or cut a deal after the Houthis’ west coast advance, especially without major external support from the US or its Mecca Agreement allies,” Brumfield said.

The other choice for Saudi leaders would be to follow the UAE in adopting a more hardline stance against Iran and its allies. A major escalation would be the involvement of Saudi ground forces in Yemen, “something Riyadh has been very hesitant to do for over a decade”.

articles.title: I've battled gangs for decades. Now I'm fighting a threat that's even harder
articles.summary: Drill rap livestreams on smartphones are leading to shootings and funerals on Chicago's South Side, where location tags become deadly dares.
articles.body: In my time on the South Side of Chicago, I’ve asked people to look at what we’re losing. I have pointed out the root causes of gun violence, set up programs to counter it, confronted gangsters and brought them to truces, and helped many enter mainstream society as productive citizens. I’ve created after-school programs to counter our failing public schools so that kids won’t give up on themselves. But lately, I’ve been looking at another problem that may just be equally dangerous: the smartphone. When you look at a smartphone, it doesn’t look like a threat. It looks like a tool for connection and even for opportunity. And for a lot of young people in my neighborhood, it has been exactly that — a way to make music, create an online following and learn about worlds outside of this block. I don’t want to discount what they have done because some have built real careers with nothing but a phone and its many tools. That’s a genuine way out of poverty, and I have no desire to shut that door. But I can’t ignore the dark side of the phone. AMERICA MOCKED THE AMISH AND OTHER GROUPS OVER TECHNOLOGY. MAYBE THEY WERE RIGHT What I feel is that far too few of us acknowledge the full power of the phone. I once watched a documentary that said the power of all the computers needed to put the first man on the moon now existed in our tiny little phones. I don’t know if that’s true, but there is no doubt about the phone’s power. It puts the entire world at a kid’s fingertips. Where I’ve seen the most devastating impact of the smartphone is in the world of drill rap, which began on O-Block, where my church and community center sit. Drill rap means "kill rap." Some of it is honest storytelling about a life that most of the country has never seen. But some of it has become a weapon. A phone cannot love a child. It can only hold their eyes through the trickery of the algorithm. Fights that we used to see on corners have now moved onto livestreams. What happens is that a location tag is then dropped. Sometimes it’s dropped when a drill rap crew chooses to film in the wrong neighborhood as a dare. This dropping of a location is not an accident but a challenge: Come and get us. INDIANA REPUBLICAN SENATOR MOVES TO BLOCK KIDS FROM ACCESSING PORN ONLINE So we have kids watching these livestreams, half listening to the rap and half waiting for that burst of gunfire to come. When the latter happens, it is me or one of the nearby pastors who has to host the funeral. We then have to send our violence impact teams to the hospitals and homes of families to prevent retaliatory shootings. All from a livestream playing out on the phones of 10-, 12-, 14- and 17-year-olds. So the same phone that can build a young artist up — and, man, some of these kids are so talented — that same phone can bring them down. When there is a shooting, the police and prosecutors comb through all these livestreams, and any comments may be treated as confessions. Whatever you think of this legal strategy, some of these kids get locked up. But the phone isn’t only a problem on the streets. Parents here struggle with the problem of the phone in their homes. I see this in good families that are far removed from the life of gangs or drill rap. Their kids simply cannot put the phone down. Kids can access pornography even before they’ve had a chance to form healthy relationships. Our communities don’t teach courtship much anymore, and for the last several decades, we’ve lived in this hookup culture. So what does a child wired by pornography think when he or she encounters the other sex? Parents are not always right, but the phone deprives the child and parent of the process of working through that misunderstanding and, in turn, weakens the fabric of their relationship. Parents often tell me the same thing, and I’m struck by how similar the wording is. It goes something like this: "I don’t know how to take the phone away from my child. It’s like I’m ending their world. I don’t know if I even have the authority to do it. They tell me that if I do, I’m cutting them off. It just becomes an endless battle." WHAT META'S NEW TEEN RESTRICTIONS MEAN FOR YOUNG PEOPLE The reality is that the phone often turns into a weapon that the child uses against the authority of the parent. I’ve heard kids tell their parents that they are smarter than them. That’s nothing but an illusion. When a child Googles or uses AI while arguing against a parent, that’s not the same thing as learning or processing the actual argument. That’s using a machine to speak for oneself. And what this ultimately does is stop the child from respecting the authority and knowledge of the parent. Parents are not always right, but the phone deprives the child and parent of the process of working through that misunderstanding and, in turn, weakens the fabric of their relationship. That’s the real crisis. Not the technology itself — the erosion of the adult’s ability to set a limit on it. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The solution is not a ban. What I’m calling for is a shift in the culture. We need to return to the basic authority that parents used to take for granted. Yes, take that phone away at night. Yes, put limits on the phone. Yes, tell your child to sit at the table and do homework. Go to church. Look people in the eye when talking. Make them look at reality instead of a screen. And one thing that we need to do is support these parents. We adults who make up this community must echo this pushback against the phone, so the kids understand that it is not just their parents but the entire community pushing back. articles.title: Skydivers watch plane vanish from sight, make split-second decision to jump
articles.summary: Skydive Milwaukee jumpers spotted a single-engine plane vanish behind trees near East Troy, then leaped from their own aircraft to reach victims and try to help.
articles.body: A group of professional skydivers who witnessed a plane crash took an extraordinary route to the scene — jumping from their own aircraft to reach the victims. The men, all experienced skydivers with Skydive Milwaukee, were preparing for a jump when they spotted a small plane near East Troy Municipal Airport on Sunday, according to the Town of East Troy Police Department. John Bechtel, one of the skydivers, told local outlet WSMV the plane appeared to be flying unusually before disappearing behind a line of trees. MIDAIR SCARE FORCES PACKED PASSENGER JET INTO EMERGENCY LANDING, TRAVELERS HOSPITALIZED "He kind of banked up a little bit, and then, he disappeared behind the trees," Bechtel recalled. "We were all sitting there waiting for him to show back up somewhere, and [he] never did," he added. "We all just kind of looked at each other like, ‘Did we just see a plane crash?’" The single-engine plane had crashed in a cornfield near the airport. The group quickly asked their pilot to identify a safe place for them to jump so that they could help. PROBE UNDERWAY AS 7 FLIGHT ATTENDANTS SICKENED BY BAFFLING ODOR ON MAJOR AIRLINE Air traffic control told the pilot it was his call whether to drop the skydivers over the area. "It is your discretion if you want to drop jumpers over the area," air traffic control told the pilot, according to WSMV. "Yes, I am going to drop a couple of them. Yeah, we are going to drop ‘em right now," the pilot reportedly replied. The skydivers were the first to reach the crash site. One of the jumpers, a former paramedic, treated a person with a serious head injury until emergency service workers arrived. All four people aboard the plane survived, with Bechtel saying that the timing "couldn’t have been any better." "Had we left five minutes earlier, we wouldn’t have seen it," Bechtel told WSMV. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "Had we left 15 minutes later, we wouldn’t have been able to get there first and assist." Bechtel said it was the first time he had ever jumped out of a plane to respond to an emergency situation. "I’m just glad that we were able to do what we were able to do and get in and help," Bechtel said, per WSMV. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ He added, "To be able to do this and to be able to help others in need — I would absolutely do that in a heartbeat." articles.title: Photos: French students protest, public workers strike before budget cuts
articles.summary: About 40 people have been arrested and 10 injured as protesting students clash with police.
articles.body:
French high school students have blockaded dozens of schools and public sector workers have gone on strike, protesting planned budget cuts before next year’s presidential election.

Tuesday’s action comes seven months before the vote and just two days before the government is due to unveil its draft 2027 budget, with opinion polls consistently reflecting deep dissatisfaction with President Emmanuel Macron and his centre-right government.

Student protests have gathered pace in recent days over overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages. The country’s Ministry of National Education said more than 330 high schools – just under one in 10 – were affected.

There were 40 arrests on Tuesday and 10 people – students and staff – were wounded. In one lycee in the Paris suburbs, teachers formed a line around protesting students in a bid to protect them from the police.

Masked pupils gathered outside the Lycee Cesar Baggio in Lille, in northern France, setting bins on fire, according to the AFP news agency.

Bus shelters and advertising billboards were vandalised, with bottles, paving stones and various objects hurled at police, who responded by firing tear gas.

In the western city of Nantes, teens piled up dozens of bins to prevent entrance to the Lycee Gabriel Guist’hau, while in Paris there was an uneasy standoff between 30 students and a contingent of police at the Arago school.

Similar clashes were also reported in cities including Marseille in the south, Bordeaux in the west and Lyon in the southeast.

Professional firefighters, who say this summer’s huge wildfires exposed dangerous resource gaps, joined marches in several cities.

About 11 percent of teachers and school staff joined the strike, the Education Ministry said, in a system where French teachers are paid less on average than many European peers.

Participation among other civil servants was below one in 10, with even fewer hospital staff stopping work, as the loss of a day’s pay weighed on turnout.

Civil aviation authorities warned of flight disruption at some airports.

CGT union leader Sophie Binet gave the government 48 hours to withdraw planned cuts, denouncing a fourth consecutive annual freeze in state employees’ base pay as part of a 2-billion-euro ($2.2bn) savings push and a wider 54-billion-euro ($61bn) austerity drive.

articles.title: ShinyHunters: Dutch police arrest suspected member of group that claimed FBI hack
articles.summary: The suspect, 24, was arrested before the alleged cyber attack took place.
articles.body:
Dutch police have arrested a suspected member of the ShinyHunters cyber-crime group that claimed to have stolen sensitive information on all FBI bureau staff - around 38,000 people.

After the alleged attack last week, the group claimed to have every agent's name, role, badge number and personal details including home address and phone numbers.

In a statement, Dutch police said it had arrested a 24-year-old man from Amsterdam on suspicion of being part of the group, which has also claimed other hacks.

The suspect was arrested on 15 September, before the alleged FBI attack. He is also suspected of attempted incitement to commit two murders, police said.

Police said they seized his devices and found a "large amount of information" on his laptop, including "details about two murders that were to be committed abroad" that they suspect he may have ordered.

The suspect has been held since his arrest. Dutch officials have not ruled out further arrests.

Stan Duijf, who leads Dutch investigations into cybercrime, said in a statement: "The ShinyHunters group is responsible for a large number of national and international victims.

"It is good that we have been able to arrest a suspect in the investigation into this group."

Taking to X, FBI director Kash Patel thanked Dutch partners and said: "As we speak, FBI teams are actively working with partners to obtain and execute more leads in the ongoing investigation based on this arrest."

Following the arrest, Brett Leatherman, assistant director of FBI Cyber, urged members of the group to hand themselves in "while the choice is still yours".

He added: "Other groups believed anonymity or their friends would protect them... but arrests have a way of changing who is willing to talk.

"The longer you stay in this, the more we learn about you, you know how to find us, we know how to find you."

ShinyHunters claimed to have breached the FBI's servers on 21 September and began contacting reporters the next day sharing samples and screenshots of the stolen data.

The BBC has seen a small portion of the data, which appears to be genuine.

ShinyHunters is an international collective of hackers, believed to have originally started in France. It has been behind a number of high-profile breaches including on Rockstar Games in April and a highly disruptive hack on education platform Canvas in May.

The group claims to have found a vulnerability in the Oracle cloud storage system used by the FBI to breach multiple systems including FBIJOBS, FBI BEAST, which does background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which holds agent's medical records, and FBI BICS, which holds investigation information.

In its message on the dark web, the group said it did not hack the FBI system for money.

Instead, the cyber-criminals asked the agency to retract an advisory that it issued in May about the gang, saying it was "offended" by its characterisation.

The public service announcement , which is still up on the FBI's website, described ShinyHunters as "threat actors" who often "use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims".

"They target major companies across tech, finance, and retail, often stealing millions of customer records at once," the advisory said.

articles.title: CDC reports two measles deaths in US as cases hit 35-year high
articles.summary: Pennsylvania reports over 900 measles cases, leading a nationwide outbreak with the highest numbers in 35 years.
articles.body:
The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has confirmed two measles-related deaths from the 3,659 confirmed cases this year, the highest number of cases in 35 years.

The CDC did not specify on Tuesday in which states the deaths occurred. However, Pennsylvania has been hardest hit by the outbreak with more than 900 reported cases.

The preventable disease was declared eliminated in the US in 2000 but has made an aggressive comeback in recent years, which some have linked to a rise in vaccine scepticism.

Members of US President Donald Trump’s administration, including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr. and the president himself, have been criticised for promoting debunked claims linking vaccines to autism, among other misleading statements.

Deficiencies in fatality tracking triggered a public feud between Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Kennedy after Pennsylvania reported four measles-related deaths this year, which the CDC did not include in its national tally. Kennedy has maintained that only one of the deaths was caused by measles.

The agency has faced significant staffing and budgetary turmoil after losing nearly 30 percent of its workforce due to sweeping federal employee layoffs following Trump’s January 2025 inauguration and a wave of voluntary retirements and resignations.

In August, Trump signed an executive order aimed at getting states to modify childhood vaccine recommendations by splitting the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three separate shots and spacing out childhood appointments — a plan public health experts warned increases infection risks by requiring return visits. The order went into effect despite decades of global evidence proving combination vaccines are safe and effective.

A few weeks ago, the CDC shifted to using mortality data from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) for its national measles death count, moving away from rapid real-time reporting from state health departments — a move that has sparked intense pushback.

The federal agency has said it is working with state epidemiologists to develop a standard definition of measles-related deaths to ensure consistent reporting across jurisdictions, adding that the number of deaths is subject to change as additional information becomes available and reviews are completed.
